subsubtopic: IRVING OIL-FAILURE TO REPORT EXPORTS OF REFINED OIL-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Inasmuch as Statistics Canada announced yesterday that it had uncovered an error of $500 million in its trade figures since a major Canadian refinery, reported by the press to be Irving Oil, had failed to report to Customs, as required by law, exports of $500 million of refined oil so far in 1979 alone, thus seriously understating the volume of our exports and in my view calling into question to one extent or another the basis of government decisions on these balance of payments figures in areas like interest rates, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro):
That this House order a full and immediate investigation by an appropriate parliamentary committee into the circumstances of this incident, that the Minister of National Revenue investigate immediately whether other oil companies have also not made such reports to Customs, and whether the oil company in question and other oil companies have paid the taxes required by law on the income from such exports; that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources investigate, if the petroleum from which the exported oil was refined was imported, whether in spite of this, Irving Oil was paid public funds regarding it from the oil compensation program, and that these ministers report as soon as possible to the House on these investigations and the actions taken as a result of them.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC REFERENDUM-UNDERSTANDING OF QUEBECKERS AFTER REFERENDUM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before addressing my question to the right hon. Prime Minister, I want first of all, on behalf of the members of this House, to offer my heartfelt congratulations to the three federalists elected yesterday with an overwhelming majority in the province of Quebec, and also to Mr. Ryan, and I would like as well to thank my colleagues who over the past few weeks have spent many days helping those three federalists get elected.
In view of these results, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. I do not think that one should, and the Prime Minister has stated the same thing, get the idea that these byelections have solved the problem. Is the Prime Minister willing to reconsider his role and is he determined, as Prime Minister of Canada and in view of the positive results of yesterday's byelections, to take action in order to tell Quebeckers and all Canadians that, after the results are known and Quebeckers have voted no to the referendum, there will be in the country a climate of joy and generosity in which Canadians will be able to say to Quebeckers that they can expect a lot of negotiating from federalists with the view to giving Quebec a new status and a better understanding by all Canadians of the problems of the Frenchspeaking in Canada?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have often indicated both in Parliament and throughout the country that I believe it is essential for us to continue to act in such a way as to demonstrate our flexibility as a new government. In a way this is good news. There was an error in the export figures in 1978 of approximately $300 million, and $500 million to date for 1979. Omitted were 1.5 million barrels per month of refined petroleum products, gasoline and fuel oil, over the period April, 1978, to October, 1979. That means that the merchandise trade surplus for 1978 would increase to $3.7 billion from $3.4 billion, while the current account deficit would narrow to approximately $5 billion. That is good news.
It also means, for example, that this year's trade surplus could well be at least $2.1 billion which is an improvement over what we have been expecting. The reporting error is relatively small with respect to the total economy, because we have a GNP of over $250 billion and it is equivalent to 0.2 per cent in current dollars. The revision will affect the data on the trade surplus. Unfortunately, it is not a big enough error to affect interest rates. If it were a huge error-say $500 billion or something like that-then it would have helped, but unfortunately it is a relatively small error in the total picture. It is not an error of Statistics Canada, but of the oil company not reporting the figures to Statistics Canada. I understand that Statistics Canada discovered the error itself, but my hon. friend would have more information on that.

subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY POLICE OFFICERS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Last Friday, as the government was still receiving editorial congratulations on the basis of reassuring statements by the Solicitor General for its apparent abandonment of the Prime Minister's election-time promise that he would allow illegal acts by the police through a minister of his cabinet, the Prime Minister apparently raised the issue again by reverting to his election-time position.
The time has come, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Prime Minister squarely in this House whether he stands by the rule of law traditional to our society, or whether he is determined to introduce a new system of allowing illegal police acts under ministerial sanction. When replying, would the Prime Minister please give some thought to the words of his distinguished colleague from Peace River, to the effect that the implementation of the Prime Minister's proposals will mark the beginning of the disintegration of democratic society in Canada?

subsubtopic: ILLEGAL ACTS COMMITTED BY POLICE OFFICERS-PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I stand by the rule of law. That is one of the reasons we are determined to find some means by which we can ensure that all of the actions of the police in Canada are conducted in accordance with the law of Canada.

Mr. Speaker,

I do not usually rise on such matters. 1 read carefully Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, and I think the only way I can let the House know that the minister misled the House and that he should set the facts straight is the one I am using today. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall briefly that in June 1972, the then minister, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Munro), had before the House a family allowance proposal called FISP, which was rejected by

the Canadian people and was not brought back since the government was re-elected on October 30, 1972. Later my colleague and fellow frontbencher, the hon. member for Out-remont (Mr. Lalonde), reviewed the whole matter of social security in the paper titled "Background paper on social security", published on April 18, 1973, examined at eight federal provincial meetings, the last one being the famous meeting of June 1 and 2, 1976, after-

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This very important federal-provincial conference dealt with the whole social security issue in Canada. I had a number of research papers prepared which were all published at the time and which touched upon specific areas of social welfare problems in Canada. There was also the Harvey Lazar report concerning pensions which the former government had approved just before the election and which has not yet been published. This report dealt only with old age security pensions. I should like to add that when I left the department, the object of research was the guaranteed annual income.
Canadian women have heard it said on several occasions that sooner or later the Progressive Conservative Party would cut off family allowances. The minister has said that I initiated this action. This is not true! When he was appointed to his department, he stated in the House that he had found a document to that effect. This is not true either.
I did not launch any study to cut family allowances. I want to make that very clear. What he did find in his research branch was a group studying the guaranteed annual income and it does not have anything to do with family allowances. On another occasion he said that there had not been any over-all review of social security in Canada. He is contradicting himself because on two different dates he said the opposite. There has been one. There has been an exhaustive study which lasted several years, three years in fact; it was stopped because Ontario among others rejected that proposal made to all provinces.
So I object when the minister tells Canadians that during ten years nobody ever did anything in Canada to update our social security system and hides behind that to tell people it is essential to cut family allowances by 1981. I would simply like him to familiarize himself enough with that file so as to be able to answer about each one, as it exists, because it has a name, and a research team behind it. He should refrain from muddling up the issue and putting up smokescreens to hide what exists or does not exist in terms of reviews. It seems to me that the concern of the hon. member is that when I commented in the House in response to a question from the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) about the last ten years, I had hurt her feelings because somehow I was not giving a clear understanding of her record as minister of health and welfare and that of her party in the last ten years. My concern in answering the question the other day was to point out that there were a number of injustices which were raised by the hon. member for Oshawa, and indeed the purpose of my review was to try to deal with those injustices. If the hon. member is suggesting that a number of things were done in the last ten years, then I would agree that of course there were. My concern was that the injustices to which the hon. member for Oshawa and I were referring to had not been dealt with. If they had been dealt with, then of course I would not have to go through the review in order to deal with them.
I might say in particular with respect to the review the hon. member mentioned that it involves not only the question of

pensions, which is before the standing committee, not only the matter of the select committee with respect to the handicapped, but a premise which was not carried out in the previous ten years, and, what is most important, the review involves participation by the provinces. I would invite the hon. member, if she would like, to visit those provinces and ask them how they feel about participation in terms of the review over the last ten years. I think she will get a pretty strong earful.
So I have no apology whatsoever for the comment I made with respect to the last ten years. I would suggest that in beginning with the Lazar report, the previous government did a good thing and it is now about to come before the committee. Indeed the reviews that were undertaken by the hon. member's predecessor were worth doing at the time but did not deal with all those injustices with which the review I have undertaken is supposed to deal.

Questions Nos. 274, 292 and 295 in particular are extremely important. There is also question No. 384, put by the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). Despite the government's philosophy of being an open government, we cannot get answers.
So, Mr. Speaker, I demand that the parliamentary secretary inform his minister that we want immediate answers because our parliamentary system does not allow every one to question ministers every day. The best way to have accurate and precise answers and to save members' time is to table questions and have them answered by the parliamentary secretary. I therefore hope that this government will understand once and for all that it should reply immediately to the questions once they are tabled.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the farmers of Canada, as demonstrated (a) by the imposition of unconscionably high interest rates (b) by its determination to follow the policies of the former Liberal government in continuing to ignore the grain transportation recommendations of the Hall commission, and (c) by proceeding to abandon the Crowsnest Pass rates for the movement of western grain.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Members are reminded that, pursuant to section 11 of Standing Order 58, proceedings on this motion shall expire at the ordinary hour of adjournment later this day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 22 of this year hundreds of thousands of Canadians across the country registered their disapproval of the preceding Liberal government. There was no question in the minds of Canadians in almost every province of the land, when they voted for substantial change-understandably, given the abysmal record of the Liberal party, particularly as it pertained to the economy- that change was desired, and that is the way the vote went.
The key area of concern of the people of Canada was, of course, in the economic domain. The key area of concern of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) during his debate in the election campaign was the economy. The key area of backtracking in almost every aspect of election promises by the present government is also the economy. They have backed down on virtually all aspects of central concern as they outlined them in the campaign. Tax cuts were promised before the election. We have been told since by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that we could not afford them. New job-creation programs were promised before the election and not one has been produced since. Particularly in the context of today's debate, Conservatives in opposition promised low interest rates and promised unequivocally the maintenance of the Crow rate and the implementation of the Hall royal commission report.
In these three areas as well we have consistency-consistency at least in one respect by this government-and that is that never has a party abandoned so fast and so completely all of its central election promises as has the Conservative party of Canada. That is the one thing they have been consistent on. None of these promises, in terms of the negative effects on the people of Canada, has been worse than the government's

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
abandonment of the commitment to provide the people of Canada with a low interest rate policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Today I particularly want to speak to the joking member, that backbencher in the Conservative party who thinks high interest rates are a joke. I tell that member that his constituents and the people across this land do not think they are a joke. Some 50 yards from the House of Commons they do not think they are a joke. 1 understand even half of his own caucus does not think they are a joke. I do not think they are a joke.
Today 1 want to speak about the effect of high interest rates on the farmers of Canada. Interest rates of the present kind are causing extreme hardship for many farmers; indeed, 1 would say for all farmers. They are discouraging investment in agriculture and forcing many young farmers literally, for the first time in many years, to leave their farms. This is terrible for farmers, but-and this is a point I want to make because the connection has not recently been made at all-it is also very bad for Canadian consumers.
The Liberal-Conservative policy of high interest rates in this important agricultural sector will result before many months are up in a virtual zero increase in productivity in the agricultural sector. This is an observation made not by New Democratic Party researchers or farm groups directly affiliated with the New Democratic Party, but by a number of independent observers, the most recent among whom is Professor Macfar-land of McGill University. Productivity is going to go down to zero in the agricultural sector. We are going to experience long-term food shortages unless there is a turnaround. The inevitable consequence of this, and this is the emphasis I want to make today, bad as it is for Canadian farmers, is higher food costs for Canadian consumers from coast to coast.
Following seven successive interest rate increases by the Liberals, the Conservatives, not to be outdone by their friends, have continued this grotesque policy with four increases of their own, increasing the interest rate by almost 3 per cent since they have taken office.
Most farmers cannot live on a year-to-year basis without credit. It is the kind of operation or economic activity that requires credit on a continuing basis, even for successful farmers. We estimate that the increases in the interest rate under the Conservative government and the Liberal government this year alone has meant that Canadian farmers will be paying over $200 million more in interest charges in 1979 over 1978. It is good for the banks, but it is good for neither Canadian farmers nor Canadian consumers. For example, a typical farmer in Saskatchewan must borrow between $12,000 and $15,000 a year to buy chemical fertilizer, and this does not include his other costs. That means for that farmer interest charge expenditures of approximately $2,500 this year, thanks to the Conservative government.

The continuation of high interest rates means that the farmers will be unable to improve or expand their operation. For example, many beef producers will not be able to purchase breeding stock to expand their herds. This is happening precisely at a time when there is a shortage of beef in Canada. Most cattlemen must borrow money to buy feed to fatten up their cattle for market, but with the last Bank of Canada hike, farmers will now have to borrow at 16 per cent to 17 per cent interest. Many cattle farmers cannot afford to restock their herds at these interest rates. If herds are not restocked there will be a decline in the supply of beef, which means an increase in the cost of beef for the Canadians who live in cities. Those are the damaging facts in terms of the effect of interest rates on beef prices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Whose side are you on now, Ed?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Unlike the minister, we have been clear as to where we stand. We were for low interest rates both before and after the election. It is the minister who did the flip-flop, not us, and we make the same speeches in western Canada as we do in eastern Canada.
I have talked about beef producers. Let me now turn to the dairy farmers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Do that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Yes, I will do it. The hon. member indicated a moment ago that he likes high interest rates. 1 wonder if he will like what is happening to the dairy farmer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) has not changed at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
That is right, the hon. member for Crowfoot has not changed at all. A typical dairy farmer in Ontario by the name of Bob Kerr has said that the monthly payments for his herd of 130 dairy cattle will rise from $2,200 to $3,000. That is only the monthly payment. This is because of the way in which the bank rate has gone up. Mr. Kerr has indicated that he would like to purchase more cows, but a 16 per cent interest rate on a $2,000 cow means $320 in interest charges alone. He has concluded that he will not expand his herd. This conclusion means only one thing for the Canadian consumer, and that is that with fewer cows producing-there will be less milk and therefore the price of milk to the Canadian consumers in the cities will go up, thanks again to the Conservative government's high interest rate policy.
I would like now to turn to the typical western wheat farmer who is operating a combine that costs anywhere from between $50,000 and $100,000. He, too, is paying an interest rate on the loan for this machinery of 16 per cent to 17 per cent. For many such farmers the interest rate on that kind of capital investment makes it virtually impossible for them to expand. If the output by Canadian farmers declines in the coming year, as we are being told by experts outside the House of Commons, it will be as a direct result of this insane high interest rate policy of the Conservative government. In terms of the long-range development of our country and the kinds of com-
November 15, 1979

munities we want to maintain and expand, and as bad as the situation is for the established farmer, it is virtually calamitous for the young farmer who is just starting out. For the young farmer in western Canada just starting out, the high interest rates make the venture almost prohibitive.
Approximately two weeks ago 1 visited the community of Weldon, Saskatchewan. 1 had one of the most moving experiences of my life there while talking to an older farmer in his early sixties. He was telling me about his son who was interested in starting his own farming operation. This gentleman spoke with great directness and simplicity about how just a month ago his son had plans of going into farming, but after the last interest rate increase he had decided that he could no longer afford it. 1 do not claim to have any direct experience with farming, but 1 have tried to learn about the problems which farmers face. 1 would like to put on record the reason why a young farmer on the prairies today cannot go into farming with the current interest rate being as high as it is.
A typical young farmer, such as the young farmer I just mentioned, would start out by purchasing probably one section of land. For those of us in the east who are more accustomed to talking in acres, that means 640 acres. That is a humble beginning in the prairies in grain farming. The going rate per acre is $500, so the total cost of the section would be $320,000. If this young farmer was able to get a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation at 12 per cent interest, which is 3 per cent below what he or she would be paying the banks, the interest charges alone would be $38,400 a year.
Let us assume that this man gets under way in spite of these costs and he produces the average long term yield of a farm in Saskatchewan of 23 bushels per acre. Let us also assume that he is using 60 per cent of his land and leaving the rest in fallow. The total net revenue if he or she gets $5.50 a bushel would be $48,576. If we take this young farmer's annual interest charge of $38,400 and subtract it from his or her net revenue of $48,576, he or she is left with-and I am sure that even the cabinet ministers on the other side can make this calculation-a balance of $10,176.
Some people might quickly conclude that the $10,176 is his profit, but I have not included what this young farmer would be putting out if he or she were buying equipment. If he or she were to buy the minimum equipment necessary, it would cost approximately $75,000 and $10,000 a year for the interest charges. If we subtract the $10,000 he or she pays for interest charges from his balance of $10,176, the young farmer is left with $176 for a year's work. That is $176 for a year's work, without having talked about what he would have to spend for fertilizers or chemicals, or any other costs.
The conclusion is obvious and tragic for those of us in this country who believe that we should perpetuate a small, efficient farming operation. The conclusion is that because of the high interest rate policy of this government, young Canadians cannot go into farming. That is the conclusion, Mr. Speaker.
Grain Transportation
Understandably, all farm organizations across the country have blasted the Conservative party for its high interest rate policy. These include the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, The National Farmers Union and the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, to name three. The National Farmers Union just recently petitioned the Minister of Finance asking him to reduce interest rates. 1 hope at long last he will respond to that.
On the interest rate question, Mr. Speaker, this House has discussed many times already its direct effects on urban Canadians-the direct effects of driving up the cost of housing, the cost of living in every respect. I have tried briefly to show that, bad as it has been for those in urban Canada, it has become a disaster in rural Canada. It is time for the Tories to live up to their election promise and bring down the interest rate structure in Canada.
I want to turn now to another central area of concern for the farmers in our country. Before the election it was an area of expressed concern for the Conservative party. I refer to the Hall royal commission. I should like to put on record what some notable Conservative had to say before the election. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) called the Hall report the "Magna Carta" of the west.
In a speech to this House in May last year the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Hnatyshyn) said that the Crown rate should be maintained and Crow related rates should apply even to processed products. He not only wanted to maintain the Crow rate but wanted to extend its application.
I am delighted to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) in the House. No doubt he will be taking part in the debate. I will quote what he said for the hon. member for Crowfoot who is talking so much. I hope he joins in the debate officially at some point.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: I will catch you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
On April 25, 1978, the Minister of Transport said in this House:
-my party endorses the Hall recommendations not only as a transportation charter for the west but also as an economic manifesto.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, before the election, in a campaign statement issued on April 19 of this year, the Conservative party stated that the Crowsnest Pass rate is to be maintained. That is what the Conservative party said before the election, Mr. Speaker. Before dealing with what the Conservatives said after the election, I should like to say something about why the Crow rate is important, not only to western Canadians but to Canada as a whole.
Basically, in the national context, the Crow rate is important because it is part of this national bargain. It is one way of viewing the country but by no means the only way of viewing it. It is part of the national bargain that is involved in a country as geographically diverse as our own. Industry in the geographic heartland of Canada, in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, historically has had economic measures taken to

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
ensure industrial growth. In return for this there has been an historical commitment, certainly on the part of my party and also it was thought on the part of all parties in the past, that what was good in terms of encouraging industrial growth in Ontario and Quebec ought to hold good in terms of the Crow rate for western Canada. I want to say on behalf of my party, Mr. Speaker, that I have made that point, not only in the province of Ontario but also in western Canada. We say the same thing in both parts of the country and just as we defend industry in Ontario, we defend, without qualification, the Crow rates in western Canada.
Let me put in concrete terms what it means for a farmer, let us say, in Saskatchewan in a small community by the name of Wakaw. The Crow rate from Wakaw to Vancouver is 24 cents per 100 pounds. The commercial rate that CN has filed for domestic grain from this community to Vancouver is $3.12 per 100 pounds, 13 times the Crow rate. If the Crow rate goes, farmers in this community would lose $1.73 per bushel or 29 per cent of today's wheat price.
The Crow rate in general gives Canadian farmers a competitive edge over their counterparts in the United States. American farmers have to pay anywhere from four to six times the transportation costs of Canadian farmers under the Crow rate. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the Crow rate, while enabling Canadian farmers to obtain export markets, has enabled the same farmers to contribute some $2.3 billion to our balance of payments in 1978. Once the Crow rate is gone, as it seems is the clear plan of the government, in my view it would be gone forever as long as we had either the Tory or Liberal parties around.
Payments to individual farmers-and that is what is being talked about in terms of a replacement for the Crow rate- would appear to be some kind of welfare to the Canadian farmer. Such schemes, as in other welfare schemes when they are seen by the Tories, would be abandoned whenever it was politically expedient or when we had someone like the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) get up on the wrong side of the bed some Monday morning and decide it is time to take a whack at the ordinary people of this country.
It has been argued that the Crow rate should be abandoned because the railways need a financial incentive to haul grain. That is the classic argument heard from the backbench Tories who are so vocal on the point. They need an incentive, they say, for their good friends in the CPR. I should like to consider the effects of such incentives, Mr. Speaker.
In the United States, despite grain rates that are, as I have said already, four to six times higher than the Crow rate, rail cars take longer to get to port than they do in Canada. There is a chronic car shortage which is worse than it is in Canada and tracks are, believe it or not, on the whole in worse shape than they are in Canada. So much for financial incentives as a method of improving grain handling facilities as we have seen it in the United States.
We do not have to go to the United States to find a comparable grain shipping situation, however. We can consider our own farmers in the maritimes, for example. They, too, have experienced financial incentives given to the railways. For

example, the potato rate in that part of Canada is six times the Crow rate. This does not mean better transportation of potatoes for farmers in the maritimes or an improvement in conditions. Between 1974 and 1977, potato rates increased 53 per cent. That is the charge to the farmer. The supply of refrigerated freight cars, so essential to the same farmers, fell at a rate of 6 per cent and, as a result, potato shipments from the maritimes dropped by some 32 per cent.
Regrettably, incentives have never worked with the CPR in the past nor are they likely to work in the future. At the present time CPR owes some $679 million to the people of Canada in deferred income tax. Public gifts to the CPR have simply enabled it to make $227 million profit because of the way bookkeeping is permitted in this country. That profit is for the first six months of this year, while still owing some $679 million in deferred income tax to everyone in the land. The point is that the railway companies just ought not to be coddled by some kind of financial incentives. They are compelled by the Railway Act passed by this Parliament to provide suitable and adequate accommodation for all grain offered for shipment, and they should live up to that obligation by law to the farmers of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
I suggest in this context it is no more proper for the railways to demand an incentive to haul grain than for a private citizen in Canada to demand an incentive for obeying the speed limit on the highways. The law holds for the ordinary citizen; it should hold equally well for the CPR.
The Hall royal commission said that the government should make the railways obey the law. It said that the railways should have to buy the hopper cars and fix the tracks, and then, and only then, should it come to the Government of Canada for subsidies, after they have completed their actions. Surely, Mr. Speaker, Hall was right. We said Hall was right before the election; we repeat it now. I wish the Tories were doing the same thing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Where are they?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
I want to point out the Hall royal commission recognized that the Wheat Board is doing a good job for the people of Canada and for our farmers. It suggested that the Wheat Board should be given more power, not less power, in terms of its responsibility in the co-ordination of grain movements.
Western Canada and the NDP greeted the Hall report with open arms in 1977. None of the major recommendations I have talked about today were implemented either by the Liberals before the election or the Conservatives since the election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: You are fibbing again.

November 15, 1979

speechtext: Touchy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
The Liberals had their chance for two years after the Hall royal commission report. They blew it. They did nothing.
1 have already quoted several Conservatives and their statements made during the election campaign before the election. 1 would like now to turn around and show what the Tories said after they formed a government. Here is what they said; I have three examples. In July, two months after the election, two provincial Tory governments, one in Alberta and the other in Manitoba, suggested that the Crow rate be scrapped,-completely contrary to the Hall report. In October, the Conservative government in Ottawa stripped the Wheat Board of its powers to co-ordinate grain movements and transferred that power to their good friend, Mr. Hugh Horner, a well-known Tory, who promptly announced that the quota system should be abolished. I might add he had already indicated that he too wanted the Crow rate abolished.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: That is false.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: That is false.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
The Tories are getting excited again. One thing a Tory cannot stand is the truth.
Some bon. Members: No.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
It puts them in a state of apoplexy. The Hall report recommended that the Wheat Board play a more prominent role, as I said a minute ago, in the co-ordination of grain transportation. Who do they appoint for the task of co-ordinating grain? A man who is opposed to the very principle.
Finally, on November 7, about a week ago, the Minister of Transport, who is sitting over there chuckling this afternoon-

speechtext:
I thank hon. members. I will try to conclude my remarks and I will listen with interest to what other hon. members have to say.
The Conservatives have simply shelved the Hall report. They have been continuing the very programs of the Liberals in this field, that before the election they were so critical of. They are in fact perfect students of Otto Lang. They talk one way before an election and act completely differently after. The Liberal government did not like the Hall report, so it set up other studies to stall the implementation of the report and tried to come up with other proposals. That was the purpose of setting up all these other studies.
The Conservative government, I regret to say, is doing the same thing. We have the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) heading up the Conservative grain task force, for example. He too has suggested the Crow rate must go. Indeed, he went to a secret meeting with the railway companies before the election specifically to discuss the abolition of the Crow rate.
The Conservative CPR gang in western Canada, and that is what I will call them, say they will somehow maintain the value of the Crow rate. That is the new language they are coming to. They will maitain the value of the Crow rate by abolishing it. That is a nice step of logic. They are going to abolish it, but they are going to maintain the value by compensating the farmer for the higher freight rates he will have to pay. This scheme, specifically rejected after careful consideration by the Hall commission and described by the Hall commission, and I quote, as "appalling", sounds very much like the spirit of Otto Lang reincarnated in the Tory party. Hall said it was appalling precisely because it is stupid to send out to more than 160,000 farmers individual cheques, which is what is involved in the scheme. Talk about government waste! What should be done, as Hall indicated, is to compel the railways to live up to their legal obligations, repair the lines, produce the hopper cars and then, after they have met their obligations, if a subsidy is needed, pay it. That is the way it should be done, Mr. Speaker.
I want to add by way of conclusion two final points that remain important to my party about the Crow rate. Scrapping the Crow rate means permitting the railway to give preferential treatment to foreign-owned inland grain terminals. This could, in our view, mean the end of the line, if you will excuse the expression, Mr. Speaker, for co-ops. Second, railroads would be allowed to set high rates on branch lines and low rates on main lines, thus giving them control over which lines will be abandoned. This could mean the end of the line for rural lines as we know them in a good many parts of the country.
In his speech to the United Grain Growers a week ago to which I referred earlier, the Minister of Transport said:

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
I am frustrated at present because we are passing up sales-perhaps worth one billion per year-because of limitations in our transportation system.
1 share the concern. I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that he need not be frustrated. He simply needs to compel the railways to live up to their legal obligations. He simply needs to meet his own party's election promises and implement the Hall report. Canadian farmers are tired of studies and backtracking. They do not demand special privileges; they simply want fairness. We say it is time they got it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely delighted to answer that question. The hon. member is quite correct that during the campaign my wife said she found, as an ordinary Canadian who lives in an urban community, as a consumer, just as I have farmer friends living in Saskatchewan and in many other provinces, housewives as well, that the price of beef was too high. As a consumer, I understand that and I am sure most other Canadians do too. One of the reasons it is too high, as the hon. member would know if he was listening to my speech, is not the fault of the farmer at all, and she made that very clear. It has lots to do with middlemen in the system and it has everything to do in the immediate context with the high interest rate policy of his own party.

I just want to say that the Leader of the New Democratic Party proves to me he knows one thing about agriculture-and that probably has to do with the male species of the beef cattle family.

speechtext: The motion of non-confidence put before the House today could be qualified by some as crass political exploitation to influence a byelection in Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Right on!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
But I do not think voters in Saskatchewan will be taken in by this game, by this act. It is, in fact, an exercise in hypocrisy. In between the parts of the motion that make good common sense there are allegations which are absolutely incorrect and which cannot be substantiated, although the leader of the NDP sure tried hard.
I agree in principle with most of what the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) had to say about this government's unconscionable handling of destructively high interest rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Talk about hypocrisy!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
The hon. member says "Talk about hypocrisy." The situation today is much different from what it was at that time. Because of Liberal government programs, inflation is lower in Canada now than it is in the United States, so when we talk about interest rates today we are in a different position from that which prevailed a year or nine months ago. These interest rates will, no doubt, cripple many farm operations and businesses and cause the cost of food to Canadian consumers to skyrocket. The other direct consequence will be an increase in the cost of imported food. Also, we will have to search for more food in other parts of the world resulting in an unhealthy increase in consumers' dependency upon foreign food and a parallel shrinking of our own agricultural base. It will mean further expenditures abroad, expenditures which ought not to be necessary since producers have the know-how in this country. It will mean a worsening of our balance of payments position.
The foods affected will be especially those which are marketed outside marketing boards or national agricultural marketing agencies. There were a couple of good articles in one of the western papers I was looking at the other day-the Western Producer dated October 25. One of them carried the headline "PCs say Whoa to some Liberal Ag Projects". You know, they should be speeding ahead with some of them- most of them they are just carrying on. If they were speeding ahead with some of them-for instance, harmonization of stabilization-the farmers would get 100 per cent of the cost of production. They would not necessarily make any money but at least they would not fall behind; they would maintain the status quo, because one of the basic things used in harmonization of stabilization is the interest rate and it figures in the costing formula.
The other agencies which have a cost-pricing formula and which have stayed below the national inflation rate are concerned with products which are being grown, produced and marketed under national agencies in this country. Some of them are not under national agencies, they are under provincial agencies, but those pricing formulas make sure that the products stay in production. It is the producers who fall outside what is called the great free market system who will back off and quit producing; some of them are in dire trouble at the present time.
Unless the government wakes up and, more particularly, unless the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) begins to realize that high interest rates are no joke, unless he realizes that the
November 15. 1979

crushing burden he is placing on food producers in this country will seriously weaken the ability of our farmers to supply Canadians in all security, unless he is willing to quit his smart alec remarks and, instead, redress the untenable situation in which he is placing farmers, the farmers and consumers of Canada will have his hide. I do not know what they will do with it, but they will have his hide, that's for sure. Does the government realize that farm businesses and farm operations today are run on 50 per cent or more of open-ended loans? Only yesterday a farmer feeding cattle in southwestern Ontario indicated he had lost $20,000 solely as a result of increased interest rates charged him by his bank since the government took office in June. He does not know what he is going to do.
I invite members opposite to do a little calculating on the basis of the 16 per cent rate presently paid by farmers. A feeder with 250 steers at 400 pounds who had to pay $1.20 a pound to purchase the animals faces an operating open-ended loan costing almost $20,000 a year. That feeder will have to try to get $19,200 to be exact, from the sale of his fattened cattle to send to the banks without any relationship to his competence as a farmer. Nothing for his work, nothing for his feed and so on. He has to make close to $20,000 for the banks before anything else comes back to him. Is he going to be working for nothing? The government said this would not happen, but that is what is going to happen. Either our farmers across the land are going to get a beating they never imagined, one they never imagined they would have to face under the previous administration, or Canadian consumers will face an unwarranted jump in their food costs.
1 wish the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. McGrath) was in the House today. I remember when he was on this side of the House as critic in the field of consumer affairs. Boy, when eggs went up a cent a dozen did he raise Cain in this House! Did he make a lot of noise! And, boy, is he quiet today! Yet that is infantile alongside what this is doing to the cost of food and the way in which it is going to hurt production and people. The very thing that he condemned, the egg marketing board, for instance, is one which has the cost-pricing formula installed in it which guarantees there will be eggs produced in Canada under that system and that producers will make a profit if they are efficient.
The hon. member asked about beef. The economic developments that took place in connection with beef should have never happened as far as I am concerned. But do not blame the government for it because I can remember going into cabinet meetings here and receiving telegrams from every beef producing organization. They were not all the same, but practically all of them said the same thing: "Don't let Whelan do anything for the cow-calf producers; don't let him intervene at all." My colleagues went along with that view. But I was up in that great area of Prince Albert the other day and 1 can say this to the Conservative members: a former member of the executive of the late right hon. member's constituency organization was my escort for one day. The next day two young people who before that were strong NDP supporters were my
Grain Transportation
escorts. So I am just saying that in that area they know what we did. This is why I say that this motion is full of hypocrisy and fault. It is because of the very things which were done.
The Western Grain Stabilization Act was condemned by them. It is heralded by those who joined it voluntarily as one of the greatest things ever to hit the west because farmers are getting their cheques for their crops. They know what good it has been. The NDP say nothing was done, that there was no care and that no concern was shown for farmers. That is not true because the Western Grain Stabilization Act is looked upon as one of the greatest things, and the harmonization of stabilization would be doing the same thing, perhaps not to the great extent that the Western Grain Stabilization Act is helping those farmers who suffered depressed prices a year or so ago, but it had that same principle involved in it, that it would be voluntary for them to join. Again, what happened? Beef producers said, "Don't get involved in that; we are going to get over-production of beef'.
What is happening to beef farmers today? As late as last night in the area of Wellington and Waterloo where I was, a farmer came to me and said: "My son-in-law is being helped both by myself and by his father. He already has a debt. He knows that just the interest rates on the cattle he has bought for the feedlot amount to $40,000 before he gets a penny for himself'. The price of finished beef is not as high as it should be to give returns for the capital outlay that is involved.
1 just want to say that I am concerned about some of the statements which have been made here. It would be one thing if interest was the only cost increase that producers and consumers have to face, but this government seems to be hell-bent on hitting Canadians with a double whammy by cranking up the rate of energy costs twice as fast or even faster than the previous administration was prepared to do. This is a costly, costly thing.
There are some countries in the world which have special programs for energy used in food production. Some of them have costs as low as 17 cents a gallon for the diesel fuel used in food production. 1 understand that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) has once more been convinced by Premier Lougheed that the latter's stand on the need for higher energy costs and on the distribution of income resulting from these higher prices is correct. What kind of leadership is that? Never have so many Canadians been sold down the river of convenience by one man for the benefit of partisan gain. I almost feel as if I am a citizen of a foreign country, not because of the Parti Quebecois problem in the land and not because of the tough bargaining Premier Lougheed is able to put up for his people and province, but because of the weakness of this present government-its shameful posturing which is inconsistent with the facts, its inability to bring home the bacon when the going gets tough and its naivete in having even the bacon which was on its plate taken away through sheer incompetence.
But enough of that, Mr. Speaker. Let us just turn to grain transportation for a while. When I think of some of the things

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
which have been said and read some of the speeches which are being prepared by the ministers and others I am concerned. You would almost think nothing had been done before.
I return again to the limp, hollow and inaccurate NDP motion before the House, because it almost says the same thing. The NDP knows very well that the previous administration was effective in improving grain transportation since 1973. We acted and put in place useful helpful programs, while at the same time studying the possibility of further improvement. This government seems to think it is enough to appoint committees and negotiate away advantages.
It was way back in 1973 that a Liberal government started by acquiring rolling stock, without which grain movement in this country would not only have some problems but would in fact be in serious trouble. The government started by buying 2,000 grain hopper cars in 1973. By last year 8,000 were delivered with an average 3,000 bushel capacity. That makes an increase of rolling stock capable of moving an extra 24 million bushels of grain.
If we took all the rolling stock used for grain, they could carry 36 million bushels if they were all loaded at once. Just imagine! That is about ten million bushels more than the total storage capacity on the west coast. Rolling stock, rolling grain containers, rolling grain elevators-whatever you want to call them-are there. I am not saying there is not a need or some need to co-ordinate this in a better fashion to move it more quickly, but there has been this accomplishment.
That effort was accompanied by pressure being put on the railways to improve their turnaround of cars, which in fact improved from a 21-day cycle in 1974 to an 18-day cycle this year, with the possibility of another day being knocked off by next year. That exercise in itself increased rolling stock capacity by another 20 per cent. At the same time the Liberal government spent $100 million in 1977-78, $70 million in 1978-79 and committed $70 million this year for 1979-80 to rehabilitation of rails and beds to improve the movement of grain to home and export markets.
When I think of some of the things which have been said and some of the claims which are being made, I think it is almost like a cook in a kitchen baking a cake and preparing the icing. Then somebody comes in, puts the icing on the cake and says, "We did it all". Practically all this government is doing in some instances is putting the icing on the cake. In some instances it is missing part of the cake with the icing, as far as I am concerned, by not following up the programs which were installed by the former Liberal government.
These efforts were made in the full knowledge that the Crowsnest rates-whether you are for them or against them- have left a huge problem of deferred maintenance to be dealt with. My point is, rather than watch the grain movement in this country decline year by year while studying every aspect of how to deal with the Crowsnest rate problem fairly and to the benefit of producers, a Liberal administration acted to the point where in fact almost one billion bushels of grain have been moved on a yearly basis over the last five years. That is a lot of grain. At today's prices that represents the movement of
(Mr. Whelan.]
that product, by a small "c" conservative estimate, in an amount far exceeding $5 billion.
Then Dr. Hugh Horner was appointed. I knew Dr. Hugh Horner when he was a Conservative member of Parliament. I knew Dr. Hugh Horner when he was a Conservative minister of agriculture. 1 knew Dr. Hugh Horner when he was a Conservative minister of transport and deputy premier. I never knew him as a transport expert. I knew him as a politician, and a Conservative politician. I do not think he knows any more about a train than a former member of Parliament, who was removed from the chairmanship of the board of Air Canada, Mr. Mackasey, knew about a plane, as far as that goes. Dr. Hugh Horner is being paid $75,000 a year, more than the Prime Minister, to run around and tell them how to shunt cars. The other day in Toronto he said that he finds the CPR and the CNR main lines the best in all of North America. We have known that for a long time. He has already received pretty near a month's pay to tell us what we knew. I think that is great. One of the greatest things I know about Dr. Hugh Horner is his brother.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Tell us more.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
A further 2,000 hopper cars have been acquired by the Canadian Wheat Board, and what is this government doing about hopper cars? Get this, it is going to rent some hopper cars! Ain't that great? The Liberal government bought them and paid for them. The previous minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board got the Canadian Wheat Board involved and bought cars, but the Conservative government which claims it is doing so much, is out renting cars. Can you imagine?
The western provinces will acquire 2,400 hopper cars by the end of 1981. That wealthy Conservative government of Alberta is going to contribute 1,000. It has more than $6 billion in a heritage fund that it does not know what to do with. Hon. members opposite know as well as I that Peter does not know what to do with that. If I were minister of transport in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, I would go to Peter and say, "Come on, Peter, you can do better than that". I am sure he would listen to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) because the minister is from Vegreville and is respected tremendously in that area. I know of the tremendous respect he has in the House and I know that if the Minister of Transport, who is that member, went to Peter and said: "Look, you can do more", I am sure he would, because I am sure he would talk to the Minister of Transport. I had the impression that there was no communication between the first minister of Alberta and the first minister of Canada, and there seems to be a lack of will to communicate, from what we have seen of events in Saskatoon last night after three hours of discussion. Certainly it did not sound very progressive to me, that's for sure.
But let us go now to the political allies of this party.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Hurray!
November 15, 1979

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: In Saskatchewan they fired the best cabinet minister they had.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: They fired one of the most honest men in western Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: They fired him for no good reason. The premier wanted him to say he was sick, but he was as healthy as the Leader of the New Democratic Party ever was, and he knows a hell of lot more about farming than he does. He was born and raised on a farm and he worked in a factory, so he knows of what he speaks. He knows practically all the people in Saskatchewan, but they fired him because he would not resign on the ground of ill health. So then he resigned his seat. I was appalled when I went to Prince Albert and the NDPers said, "But your brother resigned, he was not fired." What a bunch of malarkey, what a bunch of boondoggling! That guy had given his whole life to that party from the time he was 18, but he was fired for no reason at all.

But what did the province of Saskatchewan do? They are going to supply 1,000 cars. They got into the act too. They are the political allies of the party which put forward this hypocritical motion. They are the province which stands to gain most from improved grain transportation because of its geographic location and the importance of grain production to that province. They will only supply 1,000 cars. They have the lowest rate of unemployment of any province in Canada, probably because, as 1 was told the other day, the unemployed there have moved to Alberta.
The Liberal administration between 1974 and 1978 spent some $280 million on hopper car and boxcar repairs. At the same time, railroad rehabilitation subsidies from 1977 to 1980 equalled $240 million; the expenditures on improvements of grain movement through the port of Churchill between 1968 and 1978 were almost $16 million; and branch line subsidies between 1971 and 1978 amounted to $602 million.
Hon. members know full well the efforts the Liberal administration has made to export grain out of the west coast, both in Vancouver and Prince Rupert, B.C. The Minister of Transport knows full well that what he signed with regard to
Grain Transportation
Prince Rupert, etc., was all ready for him. All he had to do was to get the pen. 1 was involved in some of those negotiations. Perhaps even I could have got as much from Peter on that deal, 1 do not know, but I did not see any great advances being made by the new minister over and above the agreement that was negotiated at the time the election took place.
The unfortunate shipping accident disrupting the improved rate of grain exports is not being handled with sufficient dispatch by this government. I want to tell the minister that he had better cross his fingers because some farmers think that, because there is demurrage to pay on ships waiting as a result of that railroad bridge having been damaged and the inadequacy either of the ship's captain or the pilots supplied by the Canadian government, they will have to pay that demurrage. I said to them that the Minister of Transport in charge of the Wheat Board is a reasonable man and I know that in no way will he allow that to happen. You see how fair I am on the political hustings?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
I was just going to say that if we go on to talk about other things, this government has once more adopted the policy of appointing a grain transportation co-ordinator, and that is encouraging. But partisan Conservative task forces, such as the grain movement task force named by the Minister of Transport in July, are unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. You can expect that sort of thing in a totalitarian type of system where there is only one party. You see that in other parts of the world. But this is an all party Parliament.
People are under the impression that that task force is a parliamentary committee. It is not a parliamentary committee, it is a caucus Tory group of politicians who are using government employees to help them. I never remember that being done, Mr. Speaker. It is just unacceptable. It is blatant partisan boondoggling reminiscent of the Ontario Conservative government's tactics, and it brings into question the privilege of members of this House. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schel-lenberger) should not have been given the privilege of constituting a Conservative caucus partisan committee usurping the function of Parliament.
I know that another member of the House, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier), has brought to the attention of the Chair a similarly unacceptable situation with regard to the task force on beef established by the government. If there is anything that anyone wants to know about beef, there are piles and piles of documents on hearings, etc., and yet we appoint another committee. We used a highly paid person who was our chief agriculture negotiator at GATT to be secretary of that beef committee. His name was Mike Gifford. I have known him for years. He was one of our most qualified people out there, but he is paid by the taxpayers of Canada to work for the Conservative caucus. It is a shameful use of funds.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the outset 1 want to thank the leader of the New Democratic Party for presenting this motion because it gives the government an opportunity to respond to some of the statements that have been made by the NDP. It also gives us an opportunity to respond to the somewhat inaccurate thrusts contained in the motion itself. I could not help but recognize the torture which the leader of the NDP so obviously went through when he read his speech, which was probably prepared by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: He is not that capable.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
I have a great deal of respect for him. He is the only rural member in that caucus, I think, although I am not sure whether he ever drove a tractor. But I think he has seen them. Notwithstanding the fact that he has never driven a tractor, I do have a lot of respect for his ability to deal with agriculture, and I am sure he helped his leader out immensely today, notwithstanding the torture that his leader had to go through.
There are a couple of points with which I want to deal and, as well, a couple with which 1 take issue.
I should say at the outset that, knowing the leader of the NDP to be a very skilled and competent debater, I would have thought it would not have been necessary for him to distort a speech and to quote it out of context. Because he quoted a portion of a speech 1 had made to the UGG in Calgary a week ago wherein I stated that I was frustrated because we were passing up sales worth perhaps a $1 billion a year. What he failed to do is to put that statement in the context in which 1 put it, in the summarization of the issue as I saw it.
I want to put what I said on the record because I think that to quote that passage alone tends to distort what I wanted to say. I am surprised that the hon. member would use such tactics, because he certainly does not have to; he has the ability and skill to make his point very well without attempting to distort or to quote passages out of context. I did say that if I were to sum up my views on Canada's grain marketing and transportation, I am disappointed with the past and somewhat frustrated with present conditions, but extremely optimistic about the future. It was in that context that I made my statement.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: I left out the optimism.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
I would say further that I am disappointed because of our well documented inability to put grain into the export position and to take advantage of high prices and strong demand. That is what I said. It is interpreted quite differently in its total context than in the manner in which the hon. member quoted that portion.
1 have a tremendous amount of respect for the hon. member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Whelan). 1 think all of us enjoyed his contribution today. I am not sure he was quite as well prepared today as he used to be when he was a minister. Nevertheless, the hon. member always is enjoyable and makes his points very vigorously. I know very well he is a sincere man when it comes to dealing with the problems of agriculture. I know of the sincerity of his devotion to trying to improve the grain handling and transportation system. In making those comments, I can conclude only that either he was not listened to by his cabinet colleagues in the government of which he was a member, or he was much less vocal than he was during the debate today. I am not sure which of the two comments apply.
Needless to say, if what the hon. member said today was listened to by the former administration, probably they would have been able to achieve a lot more in the improvements of grain handling and transportation, and perhaps they would have had a little better showing in the election of May 22. I suppose we can say only that the hon. former minister of agriculture was simply not in the right clan to assert his influence, because if he had been I am sure we would have had a co-ordinator then, which is something he suggested to me he had advocated for quite some time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Nothing new.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Essentially the motion deals with three points. It reads as follows;
That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the farmers of Canada, as demonstrated (a) by the imposition of unconscionably high interest rates-
This is a very serious matter. I accept it as a serious part of the motion. It continues:
-(b) by its determination to follow the policies of the former Liberal government in continuing to ignore the grain transportation recommendations of the Hall commission-
It is almost ludicrous and laughable. The suggestion that this government is ignoring the recommendations of the Hall commission is simply hogwash. It continues:
-and (c) by proceeding to abandon the Crowsnest Pass rates for the movement of western grain.
That is pure politics, to say the least.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: It is a distortion of the government's position on the Crowsnest Pass rates. If it is not a falsehood, certainly it borders on being one. At a minimum it is deceptive and deceiving.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Where do you stand?
November 15, 1979

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
1 will tell the hon. member where I stand, "you betcha". I will quote passages from my election campaign document and my speech, so that the hon. member will see very clearly that there is no inconsistency in the position taken before or after the election.
I should like to deal with the question of high interests rates and their impact on farmers. I am not so naive as to suggest that high interest rates are not hurting the producers of Canada. It would be intellectually dishonest to suggest that 1 have an immediate solution. In effect, the high interest rates reflect the problems of the economy. The government intends to deal responsibly with these problems. The challenge faced by Canada is not to provide merely a cosmetic solution which would cushion the immediate effect for some Canadians. Such problems would deal only with the symptoms and not with the root problems. Moreover, probably they would guarantee more serious problems in the future.
The new government took over office from the former administration with the highest dollar value budgetary deficit in Canada's history, over SI 1 billion this year, and an extremely high deficit in our international current account, in excess of $7 billion. These are the solutions in redressing those problems. Understandably there is a great deal of concern about the high level of interest rates. In fact, this concern has been reflected by the exchanges which have occurred in the House of Commons. My colleagues who will follow me later will deal in more detail with this particular matter, but let me add that if high interest rates are painful to some people right now, ignoring the serious underlying factors would be even more harmful to our over-all economy and indeed to Canadians.

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
Our policy is not only different from the Liberals' in terms of substance, it is different in terms of emphasis, because grain transportation has been our number one priority. It is an area on which we have placed the greatest kind of emphasis because we do know-we have said it before and we say it again-that we have been losing far too many sales in the export field, millions and billions of dollars. We have tried to turn that around and we are working towards doing that.
The other thing is attitude. We have approached the resolution of these problems employing the co-operative and consultative approach. We have replaced confrontation with co-operation, working together with the Canadian Wheat Board, working together with the Canadian Grain Commission, working together with the grain handling companies, working with the railways, working with the industry at large, working with labour and working with provincial governments.
The leader of the NDP may not realize that it is a very complex system and each and every component of that system must function well. The whole system must function in a harmonious fashion in order to achieve the maximum degree of throughput. That is one of the essential differences.
The other difference is the degree and the intensity with which we place our emphasis upon the movement of grain, particularly to export positions. We have approached this on two basic fronts; the short-term and the long-term. We set out very quickly after assuming office to get the Prince Rupert project back on the rails because negotiations had broken down. There is a site evaluation committee which is concluding its work right now. It will be reporting to me by the end of November and we will then be taking a decision. I would expect that construction of that facility would commence in the early part of 1980.
We are looking at ways and means of increasing our export capability through the port of Churchill. Yesterday we had a very historic and significant event. We visited Churchill and witnessed the loading of some 24.5 thousand metric tons of barley being loaded in the MV Arctic for movement to Poland. This is the latest movement, a month after the season had closed. We hope to repeat that in the early part of the season and to repeat it again next fall. Nevertheless, we need not only Prince Rupert, we need Churchill, we need Vancouver and we need Thunder Bay.
I see Canada as a major grower of grain and a major exporter of grain utilizing four spouts; the port of Thunder Bay, the port of Churchill, the port of Prince Rupert and the port of Vancouver. We are going to need each and every one of those ports if we are to achieve the 30 million metric ton export target figure which we have pledged to do by 1985. We will do it given the time and given the kind of initiatives we have taken, and I am confident we can.
In the area of additional rolling stock, the Canadian Wheat Board has 2,000 hopper cars coming on stream right at the present time. They are being delivered right now. The federal government did engage in leasing some 2,000 hopper cars and

they will be coming on stream in the early part of next year. There were basically two reasons that we leased; firstly, the Liberals did not leave us any money to spend on that item so we had to lease; and secondly, the matter of leasing cars allowed us to bring cars on stream much quicker than if we had purchased them, so we will be receiving these cars in the early part of next year. There will be 2,000 from the Wheat Board, 2,000 from the federal government, 1,000 from the province of Saskatchewan, 1,000 from the province of Alberta and some 400 from the province of Manitoba; that is 6,400 additional hopper cars coming on stream right now.
In addition we have renewed the boxcar rehabilitation program, which is going on in the city of Winnipeg primarily. Some 5,000 rehabs will be coming on stream between now and the middle of next year, so that is a total of 11,400 boxcars and hopper cars which will be coming on stream between now and 1981.

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
railways the difference, whatever they want, and if there is not enough from the federal treasury, then the provinces will dig in and give them some more." This government does not take that position. I want to assure this House that any change in the structure application of the Crow benefit, value or advantage will only come after there is full consultation with the producers, if there will be any changes at all. We believe that the producers of Canada should have some say in this matter, and we are prepared to capitalize on their expertise and ideas.
The second point I want to make is that our government believes that the railways have a firm obligation to move our grain expeditiously, effectively and efficiently in the producers' interests and, indeed, in the national interest. 1 want to make it very clear that under this government the railways will not be allowed just to run the gravy trains. We do not accept as fact the formula of Snavely, just as we have not accepted the PRAC report or the totality of the Boze-Allen report.
If there are any changes in the application of the Crow rate, they will have to be coupled with adequate service guarantees. Because we believe that grain is a national asset. We in the federal government will not shirk or squelch upon our responsibilities in backing up the commitment of providing adequate revenues to the railways, but not so as to affect the benefit or the value of the Crow rate in statutory form as it is presently applied. That is a firm commitment; and we have honoured it and we will continue to honour it.
I would like to conclude by saying to the Leader of the New Democratic Party yes, the people of western Canada did vote for change. They voted for change, they voted for improvement in the grain transportation and handling system and for retaining a greater portion of the branch lines than that which the former government wanted to retain. They voted for a party that was committed to moving more grain. The NDP had a policy for western Canada as well and, as I said, they set out to distort the position we took throughout the campaign and have continued to do so. I would remind hon. members that that party did not elect many rural members on May 22, and I do not think that they will elect many more either. We will continue to work out the problems and continue to work with components of the grain handling system, with the railway, with the Canadian Wheat Board, with the Canadian Transport Commission and with the producers. We will work on these problems together. We will not promise instant solutions or miracles, but through co-operation and consultation we will get the job done. We will achieve our 20 per cent this year and 50 per cent by 1985.
