speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate. The topic
Grain Transportation
that is under discussion should be, and we hope will be, a matter of major importance to this House.
We have spent a great deal of time since Parliament opened talking about the issue of energy as a natural resource, yet for members from western Canada, and in fact for all Canadians, the question of grain is in its own way as important, and perhaps more important, as the basis of the Canadian economy.
If we can put aside for a moment the somewhat blatant political purposes of the resolution and the somewhat peevish nature of the remarks made by the leader of the New Democratic Party, who seemed to build most of his case upon the science of character assassination rather than hard fact, going after a Lang or a Horner or whatever-if we can put those particular problems aside, it is important for members of the House to have the opportunity to express their points of view on the critical issue of the grain industry, and that is the effect of current policies. In particular, we welcome the opportunity of hearing from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and other members of the Conservative caucus about what the policies, programs and directions of the government will be. I think those members would concede that there is some degree of confusion at this stage about exactly what those programs are.
This confusion, of course, is caused by the retraction of many of the statements and proposals made prior to the Conservative party becoming the government, both in the form and content of how they intended to tackle grain handling programs.
The Minister of Transport was very eloquent in his defence of the need to initiate a wide variety of studies and examinations. I, for one, do not object to his using members of Parliament to do some research and investigation, except that this runs totally counter to what he said he would do when his party became the government. In a June 14, 1978, news release, the minister said that more studies were not needed, that what was needed was to implement the key solutions outlined by the Hall commission. That seems to be pretty straightforward, except that one of his first actions after taking office was to set up all kinds of new studies.
In another news release issued on May 29, 1978, the minister said that Progressive Conservative members believed that the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications was an appropriate forum where issues dealing with the Wheat Board, the Hall commission and grain handling could be pursued. Now we learn that this is not to be the case. Instead, there are to be somewhat privileged and protected task forces and parliamentary groups composed only of members of the Conservative party who are providing the only contribution and making the only statements. This raises some real doubt in the minds of the public as to whether these reports and investigations will ever be publicly proclaimed and whether there will ever be any formal hearings.
I can only refer to the position taken by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) who was reported in a recent issue of the Manitoba Co-Operator as saying that the Crow will be exam-

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
ined, that the government will move in a couple of weeks to set up a special committee and that he was not sure whether there will be public hearings on the matter.
We must be excused if we complain to some degree about the confusion that surrounds the movements and directions of this government. We are not really sure who is making policy. Obviously the hon. member for Lisgar has taken it upon himself to make certain statements of major policy commitment which, because of this special appointment, take on the weight of real significance. His remarks are reported faithfully in all the agricultural papers and the western newspapers as being articles of faith.
The Minister of Transport denied what the hon. member for Lisgar said, explaining that he did not really mean it,-"We are not going to do anything about Churchill even though the hon. member for Lisgar says we will, and we are not really going to have a special committee on the Crow even though the hon. member for Lisgar says we will."
1 hope that in the course of these discussions today the Minister of Transport will firmly declare who is making policy for this government. Perhaps he will be good enough to go through his record of statements, the record of the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) when he was leader of the opposition and the commitments that were made at that time, of which there is a great list. None of them has been carried out and, in fact, most of them have been contradicted. They have not denied them wholesale but certainly they have denied and rejected the very clear and unequivocal commitments that they made to implement things.
This brings me to the statements made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who presumes to be leader of the opposition. The problem with the Leader of the New Democratic Party is that he has not learned to count. He does not realize that there is only a group of 26 members in his party. While he takes on the airs and pretentions and the posturings, you can tell the inner turmoil and frustration of the poor man as his peevishness and verbal pollution pour out. He cannot stand the thought that that great breakthrough which he was predicting on May 22 in fact turned out to be a fizzling firecracker.
There was not much electricity or activity on the part of the New Democratic Party. They were still gumming with their teeth to hang on to some political group. I suppose it may be a trifle unfair, but this gentleman who postures about his position as a national leader when his party-had trouble finishing-in fact did not finish-behind the Rhinocerous party in the province of Quebec, a province which only elects a major proportion of members, can be excused for his frustrations. One can understand the sort of the internal bile that builds up over periods of time.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party, skilfully evaded in a kind of gutless way the real issue. He was very strong and vehement in his castigation of Liberals for their non-confidence motion. We were prepared to put one. We were prepared to go to the wall on this one. Instead, what did the New
[Mr. Axworthy.J
Democratic Party do? They weaselled out on this one. They made sure the motion was so designed that other opposition parties could vote for it. That is a tactic. I can understand their particular position. They do not want to get into another campaign because the 26 might be further reduced. They were able to find a nice sort of polite way of avoiding having to go to the wall again. When they stand up on their sanctimonious soap boxes and talk about their purity in the political world, one has only to look at their record. It speaks much louder than their words.
Let us deal with this question where the Leader of the New Democratic Party tried to pretend his statements were based on nothing but pure unadulterated facts. Of course, the motion itself contradicts that. When they suggest that somehow there has been a total and complete ignoring of the Hall commission report, that does not square or meet up with what the previous government did.
Within eight days of the publication of the Hall commission report, many of its major recommendations were brought into effect by order in council. Some 14,000 track miles were made permanent. A serious commitment was made to the rebuilding of the lines. A commitment of close to $700 million or $800 million was made to that particular commitment to rebuild the lines. The Liberal government included an additional 5,000 track miles that the Hall commission was uncertain about and brought in under the Prairie Rail Action Committee track mileage on the branch lines that the NDP, in their slavish devotion to Hall, were obviously not prepared to accept. These have always been brought into the permanent category. If the NDP are going to stand on the sacredness of the Hall commission, then what they are denying are some of the major advances that have already been made on behalf of western farmers. If they want simply to become devotees of the written word as opposed to practitioners of real action, that is their business. I do not think that members of this House should be beguiled into thinking that somehow their words necessarily lead to proper and effective progress.
In fact, what is interesting about the New Democratic Party is their interest in proclaiming their openmindedness that they are the party of progressive reform.

speechtext:
They like to say that we are the ones who are the initiators and the innovators, and yet no party has been more closed-minded, reactionary and obdurate about the whole question of grain handling in western Canada than the New Democratic Party. They are not prepared to budge an inch or to recognize that there is a serious difficulty in moving grain in western Canada, and that part of the problem is the statutory rates. What they try to do is to take sheer political partisan advantage and say that everybody else is trying to get rid of it as opposed to asking themselves the real question.
The real question is: How do we try to come up with a proper program to bring about grain transportation improvements in western Canada so we can get the grain to market? That is not a partisan statement, Mr. Speaker. What we are
November 15, 1979

saying is: Here we go again; are you for or against it? Even the New Democratic Premier of Saskatchewan is prepared to go to meetings and discuss alternatives, but not the federal wing of the party, they are much too pure for that. At least the NDP in Saskatchewan who have had some years of pragmatic politics are prepared to. In fact, they commissioned a report in the province of Saskatchewan which they are not prepared to release at this time. They are not prepared to release it because it probably says some things that the NDP do not want to hear, but they commissioned a report to look at the problem. I know that the blindness of the NDP in its federal wing would not permit them even to go that far.
The fact of the matter is that we all know that improving the grain handling system of western Canada is absolutely essential to the improvement of the basic grain industry and the export of grain. You cannot look at it in isolated segments, Mr. Speaker. You have to look at it in totality. You have to look at the hopper cars, the trackage, the railways and their obligation, the statutory rates and the area of subsidies.
Why these paragons of progressivism, who love to posture in this House about their sort of innovative outlook, are so absolutely rigid and reactionary simply is that what they are trying to do is to have it both ways. They cannot have it both ways.

speechtext: They have not changed their philosophy a bit in 35 years.

speechtext:
That is right. You can be a reactionary and get rid of those manifestos, but boy, you are not prepared to budge an inch. Manifestos are no replacement for wisdom.
We should begin to look at one of the fundamental questions that faces this Parliament and this country in terms of the grain industry, and that is the present high interest rates. The ability to improve productivity, to get more products grown on the farms, is being seriously impeded by the existence of high interest rates. This is not a further progression of previous policies; there are major economic differences. I would suggest again to the souls on the left that they go back and look at transcripts of the committee hearings. There is a significant difference between the real rate of interest and the nominal rate of interest as compared to the American system at the present time.
Furthermore, the Canadian economic cycle is different from the American economic cycle at the present time. One of the major economic facts of Canada is that we have a substantial oversupply of capital because we save far more than the Americans do. All those reasons argue for a different interest rate policy than what the Bank of Canada is following. We should be shortening the supply of money and not using interest rates to do it. We should let the interest rate find its own market level.
We should also recognize a tradition that has been quite common in this country and accepted by the federal government, which is to provide protection and cushioning when there are economic hardships being faced by holders of monetary instruments. I categorically reject the position taken by
Grain Transportation
the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that nothing can be done. That is simply not true, Mr. Speaker. There are many things that can be done to provide for transitional credit and to ease the kind of burden that farm producers and home owners and small businessmen are facing. They are a particularly vulnerable part of the economic sector. They do not have the same cushion that a large corporation has with large capital reserves sitting at the bank or which has the capacity to weather out its investment programs. The lines of credit of a farmer, small businessman or home owner are short. They must go to the bank. They are working on one, two or three months' credit.
1 would like to bring to the attention of members opposite- there are some members from Manitoba here-the results of a recent survey taken by the Brandon Sun. Thirty-five questionnaires were sent out to Manitoba farmers in preparation for a major conference on agriculture to take place after Christmas. Over 50 per cent of the questionnaires that have been returned by farmers in that province indicate that they are going to have to cut back farm production as a consequence of high interest rates. Over 50 per cent will be cutting back production in the next seed year beginning in the spring. That is a serious fact. It means that if the intention as expressed in those questionnaires is followed through, then grain production in western Canada will be substantially down. Our ability to sell and to export will be reduced. It will have a multiplier effect throughout the entire western Canadian economy. It will reverberate among the implement dealers, the fertilizer firms; all the industries which are based upon agriculture will face serious consequences. I am, frankly, surprised that the weight of representation in the Conservative caucus from western Canada has not so far been able to pressure the inner cabinet into making some changes and bringing in fiscal means to provide for the cushioning that is needed. We are not talking about massive expenditures of money. We are talking about a transitional period, and easing of terms for a short period until the rates come down. This is something which has been done before. We are not breaking new ground. Such measures are necessary, now.
I cannot accept the argument put forward again by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), or by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie), that the reason the government makes the decisions it does is because of the heavy deficits left by the previous government. Hon. members opposite have had six months in which to bring in their own policies, yet the only policy they have talked about is to add to the deficit for this year's $575 million for the mortgage credit plan. They are not talking about reducing the deficit, they are talking about adding to it.
How can they castigate the former government when they are proposing to add to the debt? They can't have it both ways. You can't have a minister of the Crown get up and say, "Boy, those Grits left us with this deficit and we can't do anything about it." Well, you can do something about it. Don't spend money on a foolish, economic program. Don't spend money on

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
a program which has no economic impact. Don't simply fall sway to the Svengali of the Senate who tells the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) he has to live up to his promises so as to look macho or something.
The fact is that the government is committed to heavier deficit spending purely and simply for political purposes so that it can look strong and tough, and the Prime Minister can pretend he is John Wayne when he is out in Alberta, or something. The fact is, you are adding to the deficit. You are committing the federal government to expenditures close to $3 billion over the next four years without having any idea as to what the economic conditions will be. You are buying a pig in a poke. You are entering into a major economic program without knowing what the economic conditions will be. If the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance, or somebody in that inner cabinet, has all of a sudden acquired the talent to see far into the future and tell the Canadian public that in 1980 the economy is going to need a further $1 billion stimulation, he shouldn't be in Parliament, he should be in a side show doing magic tricks. No one has that power, and we should not be tied into this economic program based on it. So we simply cannot buy this hollow argument about deficit financing.
If members of the Conservative caucus were so concerned and so upset about deficit financing, the solution would be obvious to them: talk to the Minister of Finance. I challenge hon. members over there: get up on your feet next week when that mortgage plan comes up for debate, and oppose it. Oppose it for the sake of your own constituents, farmers and small businessmen and homeowners who will not benefit by that program at all. That is the challenge you gentlemen should be facing, not trying to do a cover-up, not trying to whitewash that program.
Let us forget all the nonsense about deficit financing and get back to the issue at hand, namely, that the government is acquiescing in a policy of high interest rates even though the economic facts of Canada argue against it. Furthermore, ministers are refusing to introduce any form of protective measures to ease the hardship on those who are severely punished by those high interest rates. Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to decide where to begin when you listen to the former minister of agriculture talking about all the wonderful policies he had and talking about the fact that the western grains stabilization plan was such a tremendous thing for farmers in western Canada.
I just want to tell the House that the average payment under that plan that Otto brought to Canada was $1,100 a year, and when you compare that to the typical interest charges now paid by a farmer which amount to $20,000 or $30,000 a year, it is peanuts. Or you can listen to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). I don't know whether he has been on a farm. He is a machine dealer. He was chastising the leader of
our party for not being a farmer and he was talking about the policy of the Conservative party on the Crow rate.
My leader quoted from a document put out by the Conservative party, headquarters in Ottawa, on April 19, a month before the election which said very clearly that the Crowsnest Pass rates would be maintained. I would like to take the word of the minister who said this was not the policy of the Conservative party, except that I have just been provided with some more information, it was handed to me a moment or two ago. It is an article in The Western Producer of May 10. Spokesmen for all three parties, the hon. member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Whelan), myself, and the spokesman for the Conservative party had outlined their farm policies. The Conservative farm policy says very clearly: "the Crowsnest Pass freight rate be maintained for grain producers." Note the words "be maintained for grain producers". One of the Conservative party members says "Hear, hear!" But the minister says this is not the policy of the Conservative party.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: He did not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
If you go back to the record, you will find he said, "I want to make it very clear that that is not our policy." What he said in this House was that the policy is to make sure that the value and the benefit and the advantage of the Crow rate be maintained for the farmer; he said the benefits of the statutory freight rates would remain. The benefits. This is what the debate is about. Our party is making it very clear that we want the statutory rate to remain as is. But what the Conservative party is doing along with the CPR-that Tory-CPR alliance-is discussing changing the Crow rate and providing the benefit, they say, in some other way.
But what is that other way? The minister says he does not really know but they are going to talk to farmers about it, and perhaps they will take money from the federal treasury and pay it directly to the farmers to compensate them for the difference between the Crow rate and the commercial rate. That is one of the possibilities. First of all, it involves sending out all kinds of cheques to individual farmers and is terribly bureaucratic. Another suggestion is that the railways be compensated directly for the difference between the statutory and the actual rate for hauling grain. That is what Hall is saying.
If you make a direct payment to farmers, it is a legitimate concern of Hall, of the government of Saskatchewan and of a great many farmers, that the time may come when a minister a few years down the road in another government is going to say, "This is a place where we can save money." Some future government will say, "We can save money by not increasing those payments, and by cutting down on them."
Some hon. members opposite laugh, but I say to them that we have seen many programs in the past which have been almost carved in stone by governments of the day. The intention was not to change them in the years ahead. The intention was that there would be subsidies on bread, milk or what have you, but all of a sudden there is a different minister. With

November 15, 1979

regard to family allowances we have the commitment from the minister that universality will stay until 1980, but what happens after 1980? What about medicare? Ministers and governments have said to this House that those programs would never change, so I cannot take the word of the Minister of Transport when he says that the value and benefit will stay but that there is no commitment that the Crow rate itself will stay.
The only protection the farmer has is the engraving by law in stone, in the statutes of this country, that it is a statutory rate which will stay there regardless of whether the present member for Vegreville is the minister or the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is the minister.
We need the assurance that the Crow rate will stay there and be guaranteed to the farmers of this land. That is the position of this party. I thought that was the position of the Conservative party as well, but apparently it is not. I think it is very enlightening that we should know about four days before the byelection in Prince Albert that the Conservative party's policy now is not to guarantee that the Crow rate stays and that it remains a statutory right, but that it is considering changing the Crow rate in this term of office.
As the Minister of Transport has said, we do not need any more lectures about the value of the Crow rate. We all know the value of the Crow rate to farmers in Canada. We know about the guarantees which were made back in 1897 when the Crow rate first came into effect. We know about how it was guaranteed by Parliament in 1925 that the Crow rate would stay, and that farmers would have this low freight rate indefinitely for shipping their grain out to market.
The reasons for that guarantee are very simple. In return for the Crow rate, the CPR-the buddies and bed partners of the Conservative party-received all kinds of mineral rights and land. The CPR received much more land than did the Indian people of this country, for example. The CPR got all these benefits in return for providing the Crow rate to move western grain.
Another thing which is important is that the farmers of western Canada have to haul their grain to market farther than any other farmers in the world. If we want to remain competitive, we need the Crow rate to haul grain. For example, the average haul for farmers in Canada is 906 miles. In the United States it is 383 miles. I remind the House that in the United States there is a system in which river barges are heavily subsidized for moving farmers' grain. In the U.S.S.R. the average haul is some 533 miles. So, if our farmers want to remain competitive they need this statutory rate.
My experience tells me that the railways of this country are much more powerful than are farmers in terms of bargaining for adequate compensation to move grain. If the Crow benefit is provided by direct cheques to farmers, who will guarantee that those amounts will go up every time there is an increase in the cost of hauling grain, or that they will keep up with inflation? There is no guarantee that that will happen. It is much easier to assume that the railways will have more
Grain Transportation
bargaining power and clout than will the individual farmers of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I leave it to your judgment, but it seems to me that it is very clear where the Conservative party stands on the issue of the Crow rate. Just yesterday in the House of Commons in answer to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), for example, the Minister of State (Transport) (Mr. Howie) said with regard to maintaining the Crow, and I quote:
The answer to the first part of his question is in the affirmative, in that it is the intention of the Department of Transport to preserve for farmers the value of the Crowsnest rates.
"The value of the Crowsnest rates". In the speech the Minister of Transport made to the UGG in Calgary on November 7 he said, and I quote:
1 want to assure you that any change in application of the Crow benefit will come only after there is full consultation with producers.
If there is any change of application of the Crow rate it will have to be coupled with adequate service guarantees.
And, because we consider grain to be a national asset-
The minister went on and talked about the problems of grain movement and grain handling in the country. He also said in his speech:
-we as a government have no intention of removing the value of the Crow rate from the producer as it now exists.
There arc, however, pressures to modify its application-to review its structure, and there are differing views-
I think it is very clear, and it has been confirmed in the House today, that the policy of the Conservative party is not to keep the Crow rate as a statutory rate. The policy of the Conservative party is to take it out of the statutes of this country, to make sure it is not guaranteed as a statutory rate and to leave it up to the good intentions, the good wishes and the benevolence of future governments to make sure that the value or benefit of the Crow is applied to the farmer in some other way in future years.
That is not good enough. I know that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) would not agree. Were he in the House, I know Mr. Diefenbaker would be up chastising the government. I can just see him talking about reneging on the commitments of the Conservative party. The people who buy The Western Producer are the people who take the policies of the Conservative party seriously. I know the voters in Mr. Diefenbaker's former riding will be following the Crow issue and the transportation issue very seriously. The hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster is agreeing with me. He agrees that the Conservative party will not guarantee the Crow rate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be here this evening to speak to this motion which has been presented by my hon. colleagues to the far left.
I wish to take this opportunity to talk a little about some of the grain problems which are addressed in the motion, but from the point of view of the west coast. I should like to take this opportunity to talk just a little about the two major west coast ports and to urge the government, which is examining both of them but particularly the port of Prince Rupert, to pay very serious attention to some of the issues before it in the case of Prince Rupert and in the case of Vancouver.
In the case of Prince Rupert, as we all know, the former government found a measure of agreement with the province of Alberta and the grain companies to proceed with the expansion of the port of Prince Rupert. As it stands right now, there is a committee appointed by the present government to recommend on the choice of two sites, namely, Casey Point and Ridley Island. I should just like to express the view of a member from the west coast in favour of taking the long-term view on this issue.
All too often those of us who are in politics are discouraged by the views we hear from members of the public that politicians do not often enough take the long view, that they too frequently take the short view on things, and that in the long run this is costly to the public and the whole country. I think we have a classic case in point here in Prince Rupert, because the government will be faced with a dilemma. There is the desire to move quickly and speed up the handling of grain. There is the desire to save money. Everyone understands and shares that point of view, but there is a dilemma. There is the case before us of Casey Point which is a much smaller and potentially less advantageous port site than we have in Ridley Island.
1 am glad the minister is here now. I should like to address my remarks directly to him because I know this is an issue which will concern him. I am talking about the issue of Casey Point versus Ridley Island. I believe it is a classic case of taking the short view or the longer view. As a member from the west coast I urge the minister to take the long view on this issue for a number of reasons.
Casey Point will be attractive, because probably it will be indicated as being more economical and quicker. But there are some potential drawbacks. I understand that there have been a number of geological surveys in the vicinity of Casey Point that indicate potential landslide problems and potential delays
because of this. I am sure the report will cover those points and may even conclude that, in spite of that it would be quicker.
I would urge the minister to take a long look at this issue because I believe that the opportunities opening in the Pacific rim and on the west coast of Canada are just enormous and that we have to have the vision to look ahead at those opportunities.
We are dealing here with a committee that is essentially made up of people in the grain business, and yet we are dealing with a situation where much more than the grain business is involved. In the case of Ridley Island, if we look ahead at the future growth, we can not only accommodate greater grain capacity, as 1 understand it, in that area, but more important it has the potential to do other things. It has the potential to handle coal from northeastern British Columbia, and this is going to be one of the great growth areas for the province of British Columbia and for all of the west. We know, as we are more and more conscious of energy concerns, that coal is going to become a more and more valuable commodity. This site of Ridley Island is sufficiently large that it could handle coal.
We know, too, it could handle metal concentrates, and there are a great many mining opportunities in the province of British Columbia to mine copper, molybdenum, zinc and so on, which could be shipped out through the Port of Prince Rupert if a site like Ridley Island were chosen. I am given to understand that it is even possible for a small steel mill to be put on that site. The site is sufficiently large that that could be done and could handle our ores and concentrates and could in fact, provide the basis of a manufacturing industry right on that site.
One of the cost factors that the minister should be taking into consideration is the fact that the premier of British Columbia has indicated that they would share the cost of a road to this site, which is an important cost; they would share it 50-50 with the assumption that DREE would pay the other half.
In addressing my remarks to the minister, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that on this issue I urge the government to take a long look, and I can assure him that, as a member from the west coast, if they decide to take a longer look and it means some short delays in the production of the port for grain export, he is not going to find criticism from this member, but that, indeed, he is going to find praise from this member for taking a long-sighted decision.
I wish to shift my comments, if 1 may, at this point, talking again about the shipment of grain and other commodities out of the west of Canada and through the port of Vancouver, and talk just briefly about the port of Vancouver itself.
Part of that port is in my riding, part of the port is in the ridings of the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), on the north shore, and Capilano (Mr. Huntington), and part is even in the riding of the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) because Roberts Bank is all part of the port of Vancouver. The port of Vancouver is, as

November 15, 1979

many of you know, the second largest port in North America, the largest port on the entire west coast, and it is about twelfth in global terms as a port. It is an extremely important port. It is, of course, the reason why Vancouver exists, basically, because the port and the connection with the CPR that linked those two important transportation modes formed the city. We are very concerned about our port and very proud of it. We are very concerned because we do not feel that it is operating as well as it could be operated. This, in my view, is not a partisan political issue; it is a matter that all of us as Canadians, certainly I as a member from Vancouver, are concerned about.
It is a fact that we have lost business to the Port of Seattle, containerized business, over the years, and that has hurt the city of Vancouver and hurt the country. It is a fact grain shipments have not always moved as smoothly as we wished through the port, and it is perhaps a much more important fact than all of those that there are numerous opportunities in the future for the growth of shipments of goods from Canada to the entire Pacific rim, and all of us must be concerned with how we can move those efficiently across the country and out by ship to other countries.
A recent article, just last month, indicates, for example, that the volume demand in the next 20 years will far exceed the present capacity of the Vancouver area ports, particularly for coal. According to a very recent study, it envisages total demand rising to more than 122 million metric tons from the current 45 million tons for the port of Vancouver; an enormous 20-year growth, more than doubling, almost tripling the volume in physical terms, let alone dollar terms, going out through that port.
What is the problem? The problem is not one of money because the port of Vancouver makes money, unlike many ports in Canada, and the port in fact has accumulated surpluses of nearly $30 million that are currently invested in treasury bills and so on. They have all sorts of projects on which they would like to spend that money. They can see the expansion potential in the port because the managers are able people. We have able management and we have a good, skilled, and experienced labour force in the port of Vancouver. We have those ingredients and we know what needs to be done in the port, but there is a missing link. What is the problem?
The problem, as I see it, is that it is managed by the National Harbours Board out of Ottawa, also by very good, dedicated, and concerned people, but the system works against them.
I can remember when I was mayor of the city of Vancouver, when I was at that time concerned about the lack of local autonomy in our port, urging the government to examine the situation. 1 know that they did examine the situation. I know that a bill was brought in last year and I also know that bill never did get through Parliament, but that that bill would have given greater autonomy to the port of Vancouver, and in fact would have changed the structure of all ports in Canada. I have talked to the minister about that bill and I know that he is re-examining the bill and may introduce some variation of it in the time to come.
Grain Transportation
1 can sympathize with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). There are many things on his plate, and it is my guess that that bill will not hit the top of the pile very quickly.
What I want to urge this Parliament is that we examine the port of Vancouver and single it out for special treatment; not special benefits or any sort of special treatment in the sense of plowing money into it, but an examination of the picture of the port of Vancouver separately.
In fact it is my understanding that a good deal of the motivation behind the national bill that was brought in for the revision of all our ports was specifically to deal with the problems of the Port of Vancouver, and the fact that it was managed by long distance, that it has to go through National Harbours Board, Treasury Board and all this kind of stuff, and by the time you do all that it just takes too long to get through the whole process.
I think there is a very simple solution to this problem and I would like to urge the minister to examine this solution. In fact I have put in a private member's bill, but I think it is marginal as to whether it is going to come up in the draw by the end of this Parliament. Even though I know the new government is committed to giving serious treatment to private bills, the draw is certainly one that is going to make this a little bit tough because it is not right at the top of the draw.
In any case, the private member's bill is something I would like to speak to very briefly here today because I think it is in the interest of the minister and the government, and in fact of all the citizens of Canada, to examine this particular bill. It is a very simple solution to a very complicated problem. It would be simply this. It would take the port of Vancouver out of the National Harbours Board and make it a Harbour Commission port, the same as is the port of New Westminster. The port of New Westminster has functioned very well with the degree of local autonomy that one gets from being a Harbour Commission port. This means that the port would have, if it had a five-person board, which is conventional for harbour commissions, two representatives appointed by municipal governments surrounding the port, and it would have three representatives who live locally in the area, appointed by the federal government. That would give it a five-person board made up of local people, still with ultimate control federally, but able to deal with the problems of the port there.
This port does not need money and it does not need expertise from Ottawa. It has the expertise it needs in Vancouver. It has the money it needs in Vancouver, and it generates a good cash flow every year. It has $30 million in the bank, and it cannot unlock the problem. I suggest that there is a simple solution and that we need not have another bureaucracy in a very complex system for the whole of Canada. We do not need to solve all the problems all across the country at once, and this is a classic case of how we can use the existing systems, namely the Harbour Commissions Act of 1964, to solve a complex problem.

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
1 would urge the minister and the government at this time, even if my private members' bill does not surface in this session, to consider the solution of separating the port of Vancouver from the National Harbours Board and including it with all those other ports that are Harbour Commission ports under the Harbour Commissions Act of 1964.
I believe that all of us, as Canadians, would benefit from such a move, not only those who live on the west coast and represent the greater Vancouver area of British Columbia, but those who come from the prairie provinces and who are equally concerned with the smooth functioning of the port of Vancouver, those who come from the interior of British Columbia who have coal and other goods they wish shipped out through the port of Vancouver, and those who import goods through the port of Vancouver. It is a classic case where a simple solution would solve a complex problem. I urge that the government consider this very important change for the port of Vancouver.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to be a member of the Thirty-first Parliament. I want to offer my congratulations to you, sir, on your re-election to office. In the short time that 1 have been here, I have been impressed with your ability to preside with fairness and dignity over this chamber. I would also like to add my congratulations to the Clerk, who comes from my province of Saskatchewan. Also I want to thank the people of Kindersley-Lloydminster for allowing me to serve them.
Like so many western Canadian families, my family came from Ontario seeking a new way of life, and suffering the hardships of settlers in the west, as did most of them whether they came from within Canada or from abroad. Some of the land I now farm was homesteaded by my great grandfather, farmed by my grandfather and my father. The strengths of western Canada, as we all know, come from the rich resource of the people who live within it. Our rural way of life may not be that of bright lights and tinsel, but it is a life of closeness, of family, and of sharing the labours of the farm and the family business. These are the things that the citizens of Kindersley-Lloydminster value. These are the things that this government values.
My riding stretches from the North Saskatchewan River to the South Saskatchewan River and runs west to the Alberta border. It contains a great mix of people. There is a substantial population of the first Canadians, an area known as God's Little Acre, a settlement near Wilkie where Father Swares, the first pioneer missionary, held mass in the early 1900s. Canadians came to my area of Saskatchewan from Great Britain, the rest of the British Isles, and from Europe. Over the years there have been many representatives in this august House from my area, and to name just two of them, there was M. J. Caldwell, the leader of the CCF party, and Dennie Hanbridge, former lieutenant governor of Saskatchewan. These gentlemen, and others, represented my constituency well, and I will do my best to carry on their tradition.
1 had one regret on entering this chamber, and that was that I was unable to do so at the same time as the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert. Mr. Diefenbaker served the people of Canada and the people of Saskatchewan with a compassion and understanding that never will be forgotten.
As a new member entering this House, I find it a bit confusing after today and days past. What I find confusing is that I was always under the impression that debate was carried on with facts and not fiction. A debate should be based on fact and not on misrepresentations to make political hay.
The terms of the motion before this House were worded in such a way, I am sure, that the Liberal party could not support the NDP. That shows the willingness of the NDP to enter into an election at this time. The wording was deliberately chosen so that they would not have to go and face the people of Canada on the policies of their performance in this House over the last month. I am sure, too, that this debate was planned to
November 15, 1979

assist the faltering campaign of the NDP candidate in Prince Albert. I think we all understand that it is a desperation move on behalf of the NDP to gain votes in the province of Saskatchewan.
One of the problems that party will face in Prince Albert is that the people in Saskatchewan understand what the NDP government can do from the time when the socialist sickle swept across Saskatchewan and took individual initiative away from people who believe in individual initiative and individual effort. 1 do not think that the rural people of Saskatchewan will return an NDP member to this Parliament.
I am sure that it is a great consolation to the farmers in Saskatchewan and in the west to know that the agriculture critic for the NDP, as diligent as he may be in attendance and his concerns, has a very deep understanding of the situation from his past, which was on a farm in Saskatchewan. But he appears to be much more at home in other areas. If he would spend more than just a vacation on the farm in Saskatchewan, he would understand the problems and represent the people of western Canada in a much better way. The members of the official opposition do not understand western Canada, but 1 give them credit for understanding some of the problems in the east.
The plight of the farmers in Saskatchewan and western Canada over the last 16 years did not come about by design, but by ignorance. The former minister of agriculture spoke of how shabbily his brother was treated in Saskatchewan. 1 can understand that because 1 think, along with a lot of members of this House, that his own party has treated him shabbily in the past and probably will continue to do so in future. I think the hon. member had his heart in his work but had great difficulty getting the members of the former cabinet to pay any attention to him. I understood him to say, earlier this afternoon, that the people of Saskatchewan were pleased with the policies of the Liberal government in the past. 1 heard him quote several instances. I think they were so pleased, Mr. Speaker, that they did not elect a single member in the province of Saskatchewan and probably will not do so in the very near future.
There is a byelection coming up in Prince Albert where the candidate for the Liberal party, supposedly, was ashamed up until last week, to put a Liberal sign in his committee room. He is running as an independent. That is very disturbing to the strong Liberals-the three of them-in Prince Albert.
There is a great deal of talk about the byelection in Prince Albert today. It deals with a lot of the problems in the past and with the legislation presented by the former government. I will give two examples, Mr. Speaker. The first is the metric conversion that has been rushed and pushed on the people of Canada by the former government, and the second is the gun control legislation that is very harmful to the people of northern Saskatchewan and rural Canada. I feel that these things will have a great bearing on the byelection on November 19.
Grain Transportation
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and this government have taken steps over the past few months to provide 7,000 hopper cars for the movement of grain and an additional 5,000 rehabilitated boxcars for the farmers of western Canada. This was done with the co-operation of the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, and in co-operation with the Canadian Wheat Board and the CNR. Indeed, with co-operation, this government has brought about a new era in the mode of transportation of grain. This government has taken steps to implement the recommendations of Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, one of which was the appointment of a grain co-ordinator. Our party compaigned on that promise throughout western Canada, and it has been fulfilled. I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to have had a small part in that decision, along with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). Dr. Hugh Horner, a man of the west, born and raised in the riding of Prince Albert, who ably served in this House and in the assembly of Alberta has made a lifelong commitment to the people of western Canada, which is well known and understood. He has now renewed that commitment with his acceptance of the responsibility of the position of the grain co-ordinator. Hugh Horner is a man who placed the interests of western Canada ahead of his own. I have every confidence in his abilities to fulfil this role, as does the government.
In the past we have heard that the Canadian Wheat Board objected to the appointment of a co-ordinator. I should like to take a moment to read part of an article from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of September 19, 1979, as follows:
Powers of the federal government's proposed grain transportation co-cordinator will complement those of the Canadian Wheat Board, according to the board's chief commissioner.
In an interview Tuesday, Esmond Jarvis said the board has accepted the government's decision to name a co-ordinator, and the government has designed the powers of the co-ordinator to complement the board's powers,-
I think that should put an end-if anybody understands that-to the problems that have been alleged between the board and the co-ordinator.
Mr. Speaker, the difference between this government and the last administration is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) knows that members of Parliament have a contribution to make, whether they sit on the front bench or the back bench. We are not called "nobodies" in this party; we are used to serve the people who elected us.
The party opposite has hired consultants in the past, sometimes from the United States or elsewhere, at a great cost to the Canadian taxpayer. We on this side have had the opportunity to serve our government. We have used the abilities of such members as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), who is studying the abandonment of and will save the rail lines that were scheduled for abandonment under the Liberal administration. I am sure the people of western Canada will be pleased when his report is brought forward. This government has used the abilities of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) to study the beef import quotas which, under the last government, almost ruined ranchers in western Canada.

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
The Minister of Transport has taken steps to bring about the reality, not the shallow promise, of the port of Prince Rupert. At least when we decide to go ahead with a facility on either point in Prince Rupert, we will have more than just an ecological survey of 40 feet to find out the foundation structures in that area. The port of Churchill has been and will continue to be used as an additional outlet for the people of western Canada in the shipment of their grain.
1 can understand the difficulties of the New Democratic Party in grasping the problems that face the farmers of the west, as they are so poorly represented in that party by those members. It does not excuse them from misstating the facts concerning the Crow rate. The Prime Minister, ministers of this government and members on this side of the House, have said time and time again, and will continue to say, that the value of the Crow rate to the farmers of western Canada as it now exists, will not be changed. There are many things more important to this government than changing the statutory rate for the movement of grain.
We know that the parties opposite stand for the status quo; they stand for a three-bushel wheat quota which almost broke the farmers of western Canada last year. That is what they stand for and that is what we have to change. If we cannot continue to grow and sell wheat in western Canada, we cannot continue to survive.
Members opposite stood for the removal of branch lines from the communities of Saskatchewan. This government has taken steps to save those lines.
We have heard some discussion today about Conservative policy, Mr. Speaker. On page 442 of the speaker's manual that was issued by the Conservative Party of Canada there appears the following statement:
The benefits of the statutory freight rates will remain for western producers.
That is obviously not good enough for members of the NDP.
I am sure they will continue to misrepresent the facts, for political gain.
I should like to thank the people of Kindersley again, Mr. Speaker. I should also like to say that on Monday the people of Prince Albert will probably return another Conservative to carry on the tradition of the late John Diefenbaker, and 1 should like to thank you for this opportunity to speak, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this debate and I want to thank the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) for giving us the opportunity of examining once again the consequences of the lack of an economic recovery policy. Since I came to this House one problem has constantly troubled me, that of the difficulties which farmers face. Over the years the agricultural sector has become an increasingly important economic activity in terms of production and investments. Despite this fact, our farmers unfortunately run up against ever more bureaucratic annoy-

ances. We have in this country as many marketing agencies as we have agricultural products.
Farmers who have to fight increasingly complex government directives also come under all those marketing agencies. It is entirely understandable that a small farmer should feel completely defenseless against that, particularly because a number of decisions are made by agencies and pools without consultation with farmers or even adequate communication.
The whole issue of industrial and whole milk quotas was instrumental in weakening our small producers by giving them access only to a limited share of the market, thus making it impossible for them to progress. During my three terms I have had many cases of small farmers faced with Draconian decisions with respect to their quota allotments.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that farmers are facing major problems. In this area as elsewhere, small farmers suffer, and big farmers profit.
I believe this government should protect the weaker groups in our society. Unfortunately, we have put little importance on that. We think in terms of maximum yield and consider that only big farmers and businesses can and must prosper. That judgment which characterizes our development plan can be found in nearly all areas of our economy. Let us remember the insecurity facing independent heating oil distributors. The same thing goes for several economic groups. In the ocean, bigger fish eat smaller fish. It is the same thing in our human ocean.
The system in which we operate does not allow small producers to develop. Up until recently, little had been done for small producers and small business. Only in recent years have governments awakened to the potential of small producers and small businesses. We on this side have always said that small businesses, not multinationals which pocket profits and go and invest somewhere else, are the backbone of our economy. But despite this new awareness, small producers are still faced with an unfavourable system. In order to develop and prosper, they need funds. Of course there are farm credit corporations designed to help them, but at what rates? This government does not seem to have any more control over interest rates than the previous government.
On October 18 last, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced that the Farm Credit Corporation's allocation had gone up by $50 million. This is all very well. But on that date that corporation raised its interest rate from 10% per cent to 12 per cent, which blocks the road to many small farmers who cannot meet such payments.
Of all economic groups, farmers may be the most vulnerable. In addition to having to deal with numerous government agencies and bodies, to being exposed to natural hazards, to seeing middlemen pocket large profits at their expense, to
November 15, 1979

being unable to sell their products, very often because our market is flooded with foreign imports, now they are being hit by skyrocketing interest rates. As if that were not enough, they are always the first victims of labour conflicts in grain transportation. For example, the last strike in Montreal harbour jeopardized the production of many farmers who had to pay much higher prices for cattle feed. Here again the government reacted too slowly. It is obvious that our farmers feel insecure with the succeeding governments. As I said earlier, it is obvious that our system is serving our farmers badly.
Mr. Speaker, I am nevertheless pleased to see that the hon. member for Oshawa included in his motion the issue of grain transportation. I entirely agree with the Leader of the New Democratic Party when he says that the Liberals have neglected the recommendations of the Hall report. The previous government was known for commissioning reports and shelving them. If our country is to offer equal opportunities to all small producers, we must be able to depend on an efficient and reliable transportation system. The undependable supplies facing eastern producers are entirely unacceptable. The whole system needs to be set right. The situation has been debated in the House for many years. At the beginning, I really believed as many of us did that the government would come up with a sound policy in grain transportation. Once again, proposals still have to be made. I hope it is because they have something really constructive to submit.

I have stressed the negative consequences of high interest rates on our economy as a whole. I do not really believe at this point that this government is considering doing anything about them. In fact the new government is proving to us that it cannot do better than the former Liberal government. There is a total absence of long-term economic policies; there is even very little short-term action. They seem to be saying, "let us wait and see."
The Liberals have been raising hell recently about high interest rates. They have even tried to bring down the government because of this situation. How can they possibly blame someone else for their own mistakes? On the other side of the House, any unpopular move is explained this way, "blame it on the Liberals, they were here before." I do not know how long we will see these two parties throwing the ball at each other. Politics is not a ball game. Politics is action. The Canadian people want action from our government. They do not want to hear people blaming each other for the mess we are in now.
It seems that no one in this government has a say in the running of our economy. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Cros-bie) was telling the finance committee on October 30, that high interest rates were needed as a response to American rates of interest. The Americans are deciding what our interest rates should be, and we follow. The Canadian economic dependence on foreign finance is such that another country almost decides what we should pay for loans.

Is anyone worried about our debt and the interest we will be paying on it? Our deficit now runs at 5.6 per cent of the gross national product. This is one of the highest in the industrialized countries of the world. This represents close to 25 per cent of all savings of all Canadians. Faced with this situation, what is the government doing? It is buying time, and the Canadian people are paying the bill.
Mr. Speaker, on October 18 the Canadian Board of Trade made certain suggestions to fight inflation and pave the way for economic recovery in Canada. Two major points emerge from their proposals: higher production and capital formation. This shows that businessmen do not agree with the government as to the means likely to restore economic stability. Neither do Canadians.
As for us, Social Crediters, we have always stated that the monetary system must serve the people, not vice versa. The present system does not allow individuals to develop their potential nor the economy to work at full capacity. Since we must be patient with a new government, especially when it inherits the chaos left by the Liberals, I am willing to let this new government prove itself. However, 1 suggest that it should listen to the opposition parties, for they often make very positive comments which should receive the full attention of the government.

I wish to thank more particularly the people of Debden, St. Louis, Victoire, Conway, Hoey, Prince Albert and all the other cities where I was received.
Mr. Speaker, when I was a lawyer with the Canadian Transport Commission and later a member of the staff of the minister of transport, 1 had several opportunities to travel throughout Canada. Of course, I was always especially interested in transportation matters. I have indeed a special feeling for Saskatchewan because my former employer was the minister responsible for Saskatchewan as well as the minister of transport. My in-laws themselves are from Saskatchewan and I often have the opportunity to go there to see my wife's uncles and aunts.
Mr. Speaker, I am foremost a Canadian, a Quebecker, and a Francophone. If I rise to speak tonight it is precisely because, in my view, the grain issue is one of national interest, which means it concerns all Canadians and all members of this

House. That is why I have trouble accepting that a member from Alberta, who also happens to be the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) of all of us Canadians, refuses to concern himself with the sovereignty-association and referendum issues in Quebec.
If I, as a Quebecker, can be concerned with national issues and especially with the western wheat issue, I do not see why our Prime Minister should refuse to consider or participate in the sovereignty-association and the referendum questions in Quebec. If the Progressive Conservatives think that Quebec members do not care about the 157,000 farmers out west, they are mistaken. I have the good fortune of having relatives out west who also happen to be farmers and I am and always will be interested in their problems.

You know, Mr. Speaker, agriculture is a unique system in our economy. It is unique in the sense that producers operate under a very difficult series of uncertainties. It is a high risk business. First of all they face the uncertainty of the weather. I often reflected that when we were criticized as a party in power in the last Parliament, one point they failed to get over was that we were responsible for the weather-we know the opposition tried to blame it on us but the people of Canada did not believe that, at least.
There is also the uncertainty of price, another high risk factor-the law of supply and demand. The farmer has no say in the price he gets.
There is also the uncertainty of the rail networks in delivering crops to market. The very success of our farmers is reflected by the difficulty the rail networks find in delivering their products. It is eloquent that the problem which has arisen with regard to the transport of grain came into being because western farmers have been able to produce so much.
Today there is a new risk aside from the weather, price, and transportation. It is the government opposite. When I was in Prince Albert recently I had occasion to talk to several farmers who expressed grave concern in relation to interest rates. 1 shall not cite the examples used by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, or by my hon. friend from Essex-Windsor, the former minister of agriculture. They were right on. The consequences are disastrous. A further element of high risk to western farmers is presented by the oil policy of the new government. Farmers will now have to pay exorbitant amounts of money for new equipment. I have come to the conclusion, rightly or wrongly, that though times do, indeed, follow a Tory government, and if the Tories of the thirties gave us the Bennett buggy, I think the Tories of the eighties will give us the Clark carts.
I think the interest rate policy is disastrous. If I could support in its entirety the NDP motion, as of course I could not, I would support the first part, the part about interest rates. I had the occasion, while doing some research before my speech this evening, to look into the figures for grain production in past years.


So, Mr. Speaker, I referred to the annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board for 1977-78, and I noticed that from 1958 to 1963, when Canada was governed by a Progressive Conservative government, exports averaged ten million tons over those five years, while during the last few years when my former boss was minister of transport and minister in charge of the Wheat Board, that is 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1978, the average was closer to 20 million tons. So the Liberal government doubled exports of Canadian grains and grain byproducts.
The Liberal government did a good job, in co-operation with the western farmers, to sell their products on the international market. I have tremendous respect for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). However, I miss his predecessor, but I respect the new one enormously and I am a little bit disappointed, indeed very disappointed, because the minister felt he had to set up parliamentary committees.

The Minister of Transport calls for parliamentary commissions. Yet they are only to be composed of Tory members. Because of my background in rail matters with the CTC I would have enjoyed being part of the minister's commission, or being part of the Moose Jaw commission or of the Medicine Hat commission. However, I was not even asked. 1 was not even allowed to be part of that so-called parliamentary committee.
When I spoke in this House in the throne speech debate I said I agreed with the freedom of information legislation and that 1 agreed with the open government which was proposed to us by hon. members opposite. I have since realized that it is indeed an open government, open only to hon. members opposite, not to us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the farmers of western Canada are pretty good at producing agricultural products. Over the years they have been quite resourceful. They have fought through some pretty tough times over the years, climatic hard times and economic hard times. When the depression hit in 1929, many farmers were just getting on their feet. The crash knocked them down, and a short time later the elements ganged up and kicked them again. Through good times and bad, western grain farmers persevered.
Over the years the number of farmers in Canada and Saskatchewan has been rapidly dwindling. Every year more and more farmers are forced off the land and into urban communities, in most cases the larger cities of the west. Government policies, economic booms and busts, and the weather, are all formidable obstacles in a farmer's life. I realize we cannot do anything about the weather, at least nothing good, but we can do something about government policies and the economy.
For too long the people of the west have had decisions made for them by non-resident experts either working for corporations or the federal government. You only have to take a quick look at some of the more recent government policies to see how the people of the west have been treated over the years. It was not too long ago that farmers were paid not to grow wheat. LIFT, I think they called it. Imagine, we live in a world that is short of food, and farmers were being encouraged not to grow wheat. The cabinet minister who thought that one up is not around any more. He is not pretending to speak for farmers any more. Now he has an open arrangement with those whose interests he has promoted for so long anyway. The farmers saw the light.
Now another federal government policy which farmers do not appreciate or want is rail line abandonment. The same fellow who gave us LIFT wanted to transform totally the agricultural patterns of the west. Grandiose plans! "All you have to do is assume that bigger is better; let us do whatever is

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
necessary to streamline rail transportation; forget about the way of life of those affected."
The plan is quite simple. Through wholesale abandonment of branch rail lines the railroads would streamline their systems. Thousands of miles of rail lines would be abandoned. Hundreds of small communities would lose rail service, and elevators would close. As the number of delivery points is reduced, farmers would be forced to transport their crops further and further. Instead of hauling ten or 12 miles, farmers would have to haul 20 or 25 miles. Farmers would be faced with higher transportation costs. Many would have to borrow to buy bigger trucks. Municipalities and provincial governments would have to spend millions of dollars to keep road systems in good repair, road systems which would be damaged as the increased traffic of heavier vehicles would pound toward the huge centralized inland terminals.
Saskatchewan people understand the history of the Crow rate. They know that the CPR was given incredible gifts in return for moving our produce. They are suspicious of any attempt to change this historic agreement. We are all aware of the benefits the CPR received. Over the years it has used these gifts to build a diversified multinational corporation.
Let us look at that empire. It is more than a railroad. There is a steamship line, a hotel chain, a trucking company, an airline, a resource company, and a real estate empire. But they are not interested in hauling wheat, and they have already given up on passengers. They have forced the Canadian taxpayer to look after rail passengers. They do not need the railroads any more. It is too much of a loser for them with the Crow rate, the branch lines and all that. They would rather get out of rail transport altogether.
The CPR now derives over 60 per cent of its revenues and over 72 per cent of its profits from non-railroad sources. It is easy to see why they are not interested in moving grain. As of September of this year, CP investment had a 60 per cent rise in net income over a nine-month period. Per share earnings rose from $2.99 to $4.72. Income from mining was up 185 per cent, forest products were up 177 per cent, iron and steel were up 66 per cent. As well, each year CP investment expands its business interests, diversifying into other areas and into other countries. The people of Saskatchewan know that the CPR has done well by its agreement. They expect the CPR to live up to its commitments.
The CPR already has shirked many responsibilities. It has downgraded services, abandoned rail lines, and let boxcars deteriorate. When it should be buying boxcars, it refuses, forcing the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan, along with the Wheat Board, to buy the running stock. The people of western Canada realize they must have a rail transportation system which serves their needs, not just the interests of this greed monster.
The former government has taken the side of the railways. That party has little support in the west today. If this government treats the west in the same fashion, it will suffer a similar

fate. They had better rethink some of their policies before it is too late. Farmers want the Crow rate protected. They want relief from inflation and high interest rates. They want Canadian control over our economy. To date this government is failing on all accounts.
Earlier there was a variety of debates on the Crow rate. It seems to me there is some confusion about this. Some of the backbenchers opposite feel their party is committed to retaining the Crow rate. There seems to be a debate over the interpretation of words, that is, the difference between Crow rate and Crow benefit. Some hon. members say that this might be splitting hairs. To me the Crow rate means the Crowsnest statutory rate. It means that it is statutory. Crow benefit means that it is not a statutory rate. It allows for flexible rates-the railroads can increase rates on the lines they want to abandon.
As I mentioned earlier, Otto Lang used to talk about maintaining the Crow benefit. He had visions of 50 grain handling points in Saskatchewan instead of the present 700 points, approximately. The railroads thought this was a great idea. It would mean the farmers would have to truck their grain to some 50 points, and then they could haul it away on unit trains. The bureaucrats thought it was a great idea because it would clean up the map and make things easier for the administration. They wanted a bigger centralized operation. The farmers did not want it. They did not want to lose their communities. They were leery of the schemes and the fast talk. They did not trust Otto's seductive talk about Crow benefit. Westerners wanted the continuation of the statutory freight rates.
A great champion of western Canada in former days, as reported in Hansard of May 17, 1977, said the following:
In view of the recommendation which re-affirms the continuation of the statutory freight rates for the movement of grain, will the minister seize the opportunity to ensure the producers of western Canada that this very important recommendation will be accepted as government policy?
Who is this? Who made this great statement on behalf of western Canadian farmers? This was delivered by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) when he asked the then minister of transport, Mr. Otto Lang, to state that the government would back the Hall Commission report. I am afraid we are not hearing the same words today from the minister.
I should like to refer to some other quotes. Another great champion of western Canada was Judge Emmett Hall. What did Mr. Hall say? I understand the Minister of Transport is claiming that what the government is doing is right in line with what Hall recommended. On June 13, 1978, Mr. Justice Hall, when referring to Snavely, said the following:
... he says in his report that if you give the CPR or the CNR money in one cheque, they are not going to be very competent, but if they get it in a number of small cheques from the customers, they will be extremely efficient, which seems to be a condemnation of the management and if that is the kind of management we have, let us throw them out and get some better management... if that has not been done with the CPR, there is always a possibility that maybe the nation can handle it better than they.
November 15, 1979

Again what did Mr. Hall say? Also he said the following:
There is a school of thought which keeps repeating that, yes, we favour the Crow rate, but maybe there is another way of doing it. My frank opinion-and it is only my own and it is only because I am an old man after 70 years in a western gallop-is that the other way is to load it on the backs of the grain producers.
No ifs and buts about it. Let us not tinker, let us not fool with the Crow rate. None of this Crow benefit, none of this equal value; let us keep the Crow rate.
There is another quote I should like to offer to the House. It is a quotation from another great western Canadian, a defender of western Canadian farmers. On November 29, 1978, the following motion was presented under Standing Order 43:
That this House declares there shall be no interference with these rates and that they should be continued in full force and effect.
On an opposition day debate on the Hall report on May 26, 1977, the same gentleman said the following:
We do not want any more equivocation. We want a definite, clear and undiluted statement that there is going to be no tinkering with the Crowsnest pass rates. That is all we ask for.
That was said by the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker.

Mr. Speaker, the people in western Canada thought that with the election of the Tory government they would finally get some support from Ottawa. But all we got was confusion on the Crowsnest Pass rate. We have a grain commissioner who has stripped the Canadian Wheat Board of its powers to co-ordinate grain transportation. Indeed, as the Minister of Transport mentioned, our transport critic, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), agreed that we needed a grain transport co-ordinator. Indeed, he was right. However, he did not quote the whole statement made by the hon. member for Regina West, which I quote as follows:
Canada needs a grain transport co-ordinator, but that person must be an employee of the Wheat Board with power to allocate available grain cars and power to require the railways to provide adequate supplies of locomotives and cars.
It was not just a transport co-ordinator the hon. member foi Regina West was calling for, but a transport co-ordinator who is part of the Canadian Wheat Board. We are afraid that with a grain co-ordinator outside the Wheat Board there will be a gradual erosion of the powers of the Wheat Board.
What about railroad abandonment? During the election campaign the Conservative platform was that there would be no railroad abandonment; they were totally set against it. Now that the election is over we have a committee studying it. Are they having second thoughts? It sounds like Otto Lang- another committee, another study. Why not just state, as they stated before the election: no railroad abandonment. We are

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
not going to see communities go down the drain; we have had enough of this. I thought that this was what people in western Canada were saying when they elected hardly one Liberal. Don't you fellows ever get a message? I am sure the Liberals do, because they are not talking about railroad abandonment in this debate any longer. But what did the western farmers get? We got higher interest rates. I will not get into the subject of higher interest rates; it has been well discussed. The effects of higher interest rates on the Canadian farmers have been discussed.
What else did we get? Now we have a new oil policy. What effect is this going to have on western farmers? Nobody has spoken about this yet. Well, the Canadian farmers used 9.7 million barrels of diesel oil and 20.5 million barrels of gasoline in 1977, for a total equivalent of 28.1 million barrels of crude oil. The Conservative policy to raise crude oil prices by $4 per barrel each year will take $112 million out of farmers' pockets in 1980, $224 million in 1981, and $336 million in 1982, for a total of $672 million over the next three years. Farmers have no choice but to use petroleum. This is the gift, the jack in the box, that came out on May 22 so far as Canadian western farmers are concerned. Not only does this apply to the oil they use, but there also is an increase in the price of chemicals and fertilizers which farmers must use.
Certainly the government we have today is not a great friend of western farmers. 1 think we will hear that message next week. I think there will be a reaction. I, too, was in Prince Albert and 1 also spoke to farming people. I spoke to people who voted for the Conservative party in the previous election. They had expectations, but what they were expecting and what they got were two different things.
