Farming has always been a shaky economic venture. People stuck with it because it also was a way of life, a life of a closer community, a life closer to the earth and to the very basic human values. But we have seen farmers being pushed into a lifestyle very often not of their making. They have had to expand their operations in order to be economically viable. In the process they have become more indebted to the implement dealers, they have become more indebted to the banks, they have become more indebted to the chemical companies. They have increasingly lost their freedom.
I think there was an expectation that with a government which would represent the interests of western Canadian farmers they would have a government policy that would allow them to gain a sense of economic control over their lives, that they would be able to increase their own economic freedom. That is why the farmers in the west, when they were being robbed by the grain companies, joined together and formed wheat pools in order to have some economic control over their lives. As a result of the interest rate policy of the government, the increase in the price of oil, and with the uncertainty about the Crowsnest rate, the western farmer will become more dependent upon multinationals and financial institutions, and less free. Therefore, in the name of freedom for the western Canadian farmer, 1 can do nothing else but support this motion.

That is the kind of government they have here in Ottawa now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS

It is an enemy of all those people, not a friend.

November 15, 1979

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am speaking tonight because part of this neurotic resolution says:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to support the farmers of Canada as demonstratedand I will only deal with (a), the first part of this nonsensical resolution.
-(a) by the imposition of unconscionably high interest rates-
In the first place, this government has not imposed any rates in this country, high, unconscionable or otherwise. This government has come to office and now faces a certain set of economic circumstances that dictate in this country at the moment a condition of high interest rates, not a policy of high interest rates. Our policy is a low interest rate policy and our wish is for lower interest rates. That is our policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext:
But this government is faced with the economic circumstances.
Not only this government, but the government of the United States of America is faced with certain economic circumstances, and the government of the United Kingdom is faced with certain economic circumstances, and the government of Italy is faced with certain economic circumstances, and the governments of all the western industrialized countries are faced with certain sets of economic circumstances that dictate that at the present time we have a condition of high interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, wherever I have travelled this year since becoming the Minister of Finance-Washington, London, and the IMF meeting in Yugoslavia, and Tokyo, wherever eminent groups of economists and impartial observers gather, financial experts, their analysis of our situation was the same, and their remedies were the same. We are in an economic state where governments have to be very careful. If I might just quote to you a certain statement-and it is hard to make a sensible speech when members of the opposition opposite in the NDP are guffawing, giggling, and hee-hawing. That shows how seriously they treat their resolution. Look at them grinning like apes over there. If the farmers of Canada could see them now, that little knot of frustrated frenetics, they would know what to do with this resolution.
I quote from the statement by Mr. J. Delarosiere, the chairman of the executive board and managing director of the International Monetary Fund, who spoke in Yugoslavia on October 2. What did that gentleman say? What was his message to the assembled Finance ministers of the world, the 140 or 150 of them who were there? He said that the biggest problem the world economy has to escape from now and the greatest fight is the fight against inflation.
At page 3 he pointed out:
Inflation is socially unjust because it attacks those with the least means to defend themselves against destruction of their savings.
Grain Transportation
That is why we wage the battle against inflation, Mr. Speaker. It is to save those and to defend those who are having their savings destroyed; those who are so essential to society that we need to save, and see that their savings don't go down the drain because governments are unwilling to fight inflation. He pointed that out, and he pointed out at page 4 of his release-he was dealing with the failure to bring about any abatement of inflationary expectations:
The main source of difficulty in this regard has been unduly high rates of monetary expansion, often caused by excessive budgetary deficits.
That is what has been the cause in this country, Mr. Speaker-unduly high budgetary deficits and high rates of monetary expansion. Listen to this, Mr. Speaker:
Monetary policy has allowed interest rates to remain generally too low for too long periods in relation to rates of inflation. Greater decisiveness and firmness will need to be exercised in the conduct of monetary policy, and this change will have to be supported by fiscal policy.
We cannot leave it all to the Bank of Canada, to the central bankers or to monetary policy. Fiscal policy has to support it. He goes on to say:
The fundamental aim must be to achieve credibility of fiscal and monetary policies so as to roll back inflationary expectations and restore confidence. Such a change in the stance of general demand policies is called for not only in industrial countries, but also in most other countries.
I could go on and on and on with the advice he gave there, Mr. Speaker, and the perils he pointed out.
That is what high interest rates are all about, because the world, the western industrialized world, has not conducted its economic and monetary system properly, so that we are in a period of high inflation. That high inflation has to be dealt with, and that is our main enemy if we are to have any kind of progressive society in the future here in Canada. That is why interest rates are high.
Why are interest rates high? They are high because we have an inflation rate at the present moment not of 6.5 per cent, as the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) forecast last November, but an inflation rate of 9.6 per cent, year over year, at the end of September, and an inflation rate annualized during September of 14 per cent, and because the United States of America has an inflation rate in excess of 13 per cent. That is our main customer to whom we sell 70 per cent of all our exports. It is the United States from which we import 70 per cent of all our imports. Seventy per cent of everything we import comes from the United States, and the United States has an inflation rate of 13.5 per cent. We are importing their inflation, Mr. Speaker.
Because our dollar has fallen in value to 83 cents or 84 cents, those imports are costing us more and adding to our inflation. Therefore, we have to try to protect the Canadian dollar, to protect it from falling much further because of the effect that will have on the inflation we are importing from the United States.
We do not have high interest rates because this government wants high interest rates. That is not our policy. As politicians we do not want high interest rates. The people do not want high interest rates. Nobody wants high interest rates, so it is

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
not a policy of the government to have high interest rates, it is a condition that the government cannot do anything about at the moment. It is not through choice.
In addition to everything else, costs to the government are formidable. Look at the additional cost to the Government of Canada itself because of the higher interest rates of the last year or two; the cost of our debt. This year we are going to have our debt increased by something like $10 billion because of the budgetary situation we were left in by the last administration. We have to borrow that money, and we are unable to borrow it at 6 per cent, we are unable to borrow it at 8 per cent, we are unable to borrow the money at 10 per cent, we are unable to borrow the money at 10.5 per cent, we are unable to borrow it at 11 per cent because of the interest rate situation in Canada. From our own point of view, from the government's own point of view and the tremendous cost to the government, we are against these high interest rates and want to get them down as soon as we can.
The hon. gentlemen in the NDP are members of the neurotic, demagogic and paranoid party. They are the party of professional whiners, they are the professional groaners, they are the professional moaners, they are the down-at-the-mouth-ers. They are down at the mouth. They are moaning, groaning, whining and complaining in this House, day after day, without anything to offer, not offering any solutions, but just making the welkin ring with their complaining.
The people of Canada know that this is a temporary condition. The people of Canada know that we are attempting to do something of a long-range nature for them. The farmers of Canada know the same thing. They are not interested in having a small group of moaners, groaners and whiners in the House of Commons trying to batten on their problems to make political gains. The farmers of Canada know that the welkin is only ringing here today because those hon. gentlemen are "sminging" and "slinging" around in Prince Albert constituency trying to get another member elected. The only way they can get them elected is in byelections. When there is any fear that they might be able to form a government, they cannot get them elected.
Some hon. Mlembers: Oh, oh!
Mir. Crosbie: I heard somebody say something about a socialist sickle; they are socialist sickies, not a sickle.
Now, who gains, and who loses from inflation, Mr. Speaker? Let us look at who the gainers are and who the losers are. Hon. members opposite have never thought of who gains and who loses. They are waiting now in anticipation. 1 will give you the message. Here is what inflation does, Mr. Speaker, and I quote from the Economic Council of Canada:
It redistributes wealth in ways that may reflect group power rather than effort or productivity.
That probably has some attraction for the gropers opposite. It states:
Individual gainers in the process are those who can best protect themselves, shift income sources, transfer assets, and adjust expenditures. The losers tend to be
those who have little or no access to alternative sources, who have relatively fixed incomes or nominally fixed savings, such as pension,-
The hon. gentlemen are not worried about the pensioners of this country when they oppose our battle against inflation, when they oppose the high interest rates that are necessary to try to deal with it. They are not worried about the pensioners of the country then. They are not worried about the savers. Those wailers, the groaners and moaners, they are not worried about those who have rising expdenditure expectations and obligations. That is who is suffering, and that is who the gainers and the losers are in the inflation game.
On page 3 the Economic Council of Canada concluded that the federal government was the principal benefactor from inflation over the period that they had studied. These are the people who gain. Those who lose are the unprotected, and they are the people we are determined to protect.
Before moving on to our Canadian farmers, I want to deal with our Canadian hypocrites, the princes of hypocrisy, the height of hypocrisy that we have had to listen to from the hon. benches opposite since this House opened. I would like to quote a couple of short selections to illustrate how those hon. gentlemen have dumped, crumped, crumpled and stepped on the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), who is not here tonight because he does not want to hear about interest rates any more. He is fed up with having himself stepped on by his colleagues opposite. Here is what the hon. member for Saint-Maurice had to say in the finance committee meeting of February 8, 1979, as it is reported at page 39:28:
I think if we were to see a major fall of the Canadian dollar, at this moment, it would put more pressure on inflation. There is no doubt about that and that is why I agree with the Governor when he says that the reduction in interest rates like you are advocating at this moment will put pressure downward on the Canadian dollar and create more problems on the inflation side. I agree with him on that.
Those are the words of the Minister of Finance. Since the hon. gentlemen opposite have come into this House with their new finance critic and the lugubrious approach that he brings to his job, they have been attacking the opinions and statements of the former minister of finance. He went on to say:
I think the balance of payments of Canada has been a problem in Canada for years and years because we are, in a sense, a developing nation, and we have always compensated that by the flow of capital development. We have to create the proper climate in Canada to do that. It is not only through the trade side, but the compensation is being done by the flow of capital for development in Canada.
I do not mind the hon. gentlemen from the NDP opposing the high interest rate condition, but they know there is no reasonable alternative at the moment and that they are not able to give an alternative. They have never had the responsibility of power and they will not have the responsibility of power. They will always be a tiny little knot of malcontents and mope-mouths sitting over in the corner trying to raise discontent and trouble throughout the country, without ever making a constructive suggestion. They may get over to this side of the House when there are only four of five of them, like the party which we have with us now.

November 15, 1979

Going back to the high priests of hypocrisy, on November 6, 1978, in the House of Commons, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice was speaking on all the implications of the interest rate increase. He said the following on that day, as it is reported in Hansard at page 809:
Of course, with the balance of payments deficit in Canada, we have no choice but to make sure that the bank prime rate in Canada is higher than that in the United States.
That was the Liberal policy, that the bank prime rate in Canada always had to be higher than that of the United States. That is not our situation now. When the motley crew opposite moved that resolution the bank prime rate had to be higher, but today the prime rate in Canada is 15 per cent and the bank prime rate in the United States of America is 15.5 per cent. If the Liberals were in power now, our prime rate would be at least 16 per cent, based on the policy enunciated in this House on November 8, 1978, by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice, who has been forgotten and scorned by his colleagues in the opposition. He is never consulted by the finance critic of that party, so I would refer the critic to Hansard of November 6, 1978.
Our policy is to keep the bank prime rate in Canada down as far as we can keep it within reason, so that we do not wreck our economic system. Our policy is not to always ensure that our bank prime rate is higher than the rate in the United States. I can refer the hon. members opposite to other quotations by the former minister of finance in bygone days. He goes on to say, as it is reported in Hansard on that same page:
-of course we are aware that the increase in interest rates is causing some problems in the economy. We had to act because we had no choice, having a balance of payments in a deficit position in Canada.
That was in 1978 when the deficit was a measly $5 billion, whereas this year we are facing a deficit in the balance of payments and current accounts, left to us by the hon. gentleman opposite, in excess of $7 billion. But the Minister of Finance of the day said that he had to act because he had no choice with the balance of payments in a deficit position in Canada. Yet, hon. members opposite have the gall and audacity to get up and get on in this House as though we were doing something that they would never have done, never would have thought of, or heard of. It is the most shameful example of absolute, irresponsible, hypocritical drivel that I have come across in my whole experience, and 1 have a lot of experience in that line.
1 wonder if the hon. members opposite have had enough punishment, or shall I go on with a bit more? They have all fled, there are none of them there. The former minister of agriculture is still here. He is mired in his seat. He is a strong man. Let me see. The former minister of finance mentioned that 70 per cent of our trade is with the United States. He recognized that in the short term there are disadvantages to increasing the bank rate and that the whole thing is due to other factors, namely, the present stability of the Canadian dollar, which was very much affected last week by the United States decision to increase its interest rate.

I could go on and on, but I do not want to flay the hon. gentlemen opposite any further. That is what we are facing. That is the kind of opposition this government faces, but the people of Canada-the farmers, workers and businessmen-know that they have a government today that is trying to get Canada out of the mire in which it has been left and is shooting for the long term, and that we are not afraid of the hon. gentlemen opposite.
Let us look at the resolution. In reading the resolution one would think that the farmers of Canada have never been in worse stead. One would think that the poor farmers of Canada were crushed and depressed under a fantastic load. I am informed that gross farm cash receipts this year in Canada are expected to break last year's record high.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO SUPPORT FARMERS
speechtext: Thank God for my policies.

Statistics Canada reports that from January to September, 1979, farm cash receipts were $10 billion, compared to $8.5 billion last year for the same period. We know that farmers have problems and that their costs are rising, and we know that everyone has problems because of our present economic state. We also know that we are doing what we can to ensure that this does not recur in one years' time or two years' time. We are going for the long haul so that farmers, the workers and everybody else in Canada will not go through this situation again. We are going to ensure that there is no Liberal government that will permit this to go on as they have for the last ten years.
One would think that the government never gave help to farmers. With prairie grains and other storable crops as collateral, interest-free loans are available from the government.

The hon. member's government was in power for 16 years and surely they had to come up with some programs that were half decent.
Let me now look at what a few impartial, highly respected economists have had to say. Here is a quote from Mr. Carl Beigie from the C. D. Howe Research Institute-C. D. Howe, get the connection? He is quoted as saying on November 8, 1979:
Interest rates should fall substantially over the next year if the federal debt does not get further out of control.

November 15, 1979
Grain Transportation
Can the people of Canada imagine where the federal debt would be if the hon. gentlemen down in the corner were in power? If they were in power, the federal budgetary debt this year would not be under any kind of control. It would be stupendous. It would not be $10 billion; it would be $20 billion, because they would have promised everybody in Canada everything under the sun. The result of that would be that interest rates would not fall.
If the official opposition were in power we know that the interest rate would be higher because of what they have said in past statements, and if the hon. gentlemen in the corner were in power, we know what they would do to the deficit because they love deficit spending. The love what they call stimulative deficit spending. If that party were in power, interest rates would never fall next year. So Mr. Beigie has said:
Interest rates should fall substantially over the next year if the federal debt does not get further out of control,-
The federal debt is not going to get further out of control, Mr. Speaker, because the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Stevens) and I are going to wrestle it into shape. We are going to see that it doesn't get out of control.
Mr. Beigie also said that he thinks interest rates will tumble. Well, the hon. gentleman opposite will be pretty sad looking when the interest rates start to tumble. They have been pretty happy looking as the interest rates have been going up. They will be pretty glum, they will be pretty numb, we won't hear much from them when the interest rates start to go down. No, we are only going to hear from them when they are on the way up.
Now, Mr. Speaker-I won't get into this, I suppose. Mr. Shiff, chairman of Bramalea Ltd., the big developer, said the Clark government's initiative to provide tax credit for mortgage interest and property taxes deserves a chance. The newspaper article quotes him as saying:
Already we are seeing a reawakened interest in home ownership among Canadian families, which had resigned themselves to living in rented accommodation-
We will come to that later. The hon. gentlemen had better support our bill or they will be very, very sorry about that.

speechtext:
The kind of legislation that I wish to talk about tonight, and which we in this party oppose, is legislation intended by the former government, and intended by this government, to encourage commercial plant breeding through giving the developer of a new plant variety, control over its sale and reproduction for seed. This proposal to grant patents and royalties on seed hybrids raises some very critical issues and I will try to show this evening, briefly, what some of these issues are, and what perspective is appropriate to discussing them.
The first critical issue that it raises is the increasing tendency of government in this country, first under the Liberals who started us in this direction, and now under a Conservative government, to shift responsibility for important tasks from the public sector to the private sector. This is the hidden agenda of this bill both from the point of view of this government and of the last one-the desire to step up private activity in seed development so that eventually, even though it be denied at present, the government can get out of the business of research and development of seeds.
This is the wrong way to go, Mr. Speaker. Important areas of our economy must not be abandoned to the profit motive. We already have a proud record of public endeavour in seed development. We in this party would like to see this country work toward a proud record of public endeavour in energy development through Petro-Canada. In both cases the government is leading us in the opposite direction.
Seeds are, Mr. Speaker, self-evidently at the source of life itself and are the most important link in our whole food system. To suggest that this should be left, or, in this case, eventually turned over to institutions whose first priority is profit maximization, is a terrible mistake.
A second critical issue in this regard is the power that would eventually reside in the hands of those who would have the wealth to buy up the rights to whatever new seeds are developed that would greatly benefit the farmer and the consumer through greater yields and/or decreased costs. Those who have this power to control new and important hybrids could hold up our whole country, indeed, the world, to ransom, in the same

November 15, 1979

way as those who own various energy resources have threatened to do from time to time recently.
Earlier in this Parliament I spoke in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne about the question of power. This issue illustrates what I was talking about. Power over such an essential thing as seed must remain accountable to the public, to the general well-being of the human condition, through the instrument of democratic government.
A third critical issue at stake here, Mr. Speaker, is also one of power, that is, the danger of arriving at a situation where one company or, for that matter, a handful of companies, are in control of our total food system, from the ground to the kitchen table. A not unlikely scenario unfolds in my mind of the day when the seed companies own the seeds, the grain, the pesticides, the fertilizers, the flour mills, and the food processing industries. The idea of seeds bred by a multinational corporation in order to need the pesticides or fertilizers made by the same multinational corporation, is a nightmare that cannot be written off as just a bad dream, when we look at the way in which similar things have happened over the years in other areas of concern.
A fourth critical issue raised by the proposed plant breeders' legislation is a combination of genetic and technological concerns. By genetic, I mean the concern that through increasing global monopoly control of seed development, the variety needed for a healthy and reliable food plant world will be compromised in the interests of profit or, less cynically and more certain, in the interests of fitting plant life to the demands of the machine technology increasingly employed by growing multinational corporations which are now extending their already worrisome control over human life through aggressive expansion in the Third World, where many strong varieties of seeds are found but which, nonetheless, do not fit well into the global profit strategies of the multinationals.
Much attention has been paid of late in Canadian politics, and indeed in the politics of the world, to the problem of who should own such vital commodities as oil and gas. The Seven Sisters, the multinational energy corporations, have received much attention for their power and for their wanton disregard of the public interest. In the meantime the longstanding and growing power of the multinational corporations dominant in the grain and related agricultural enterprises, has gone almost unnoticed.
If a multinational grain company like Cargill had received as much attention over the last ten years as Imperial Oil, then perhaps what I have had to say about the dangerous trends in the food industry would not be as unfamiliar as it is likely to be to many members of the public and, indeed, to members of this House. We must be as concerned about concentrations of power in this critical area of concern as the public has come to be with regard to energy in the last little while.
As a final remark, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the House to a particular situation in which the direction 1 have warned against tonight, is being taken already. In Manitoba we have had a publicly-owned seed company since
Adjournment Debate
1962 when the late Mr. MacKenzie of Brandon willed his business, MacKenzie Seeds, to the province of Manitoba. This small, local seed company, is up for sale, on the auction block of Premier Sterling Lyon. There are many other criticisms that could be made of this sale if time permitted, but I will stick to the criticism which fits into the context of my remarks this evening.
There is no doubt that if returned to the private sector, MacKenzie Seeds will either immediately, or eventually, become the property of a large multinational seed company in the business of taking over smaller companies all over the world. This would contribute to the concentration of power that I have warned against this evening, and which could be used inappropriately. I hope that this trend will be perceived as the dangerous trend it is, and that it will be stopped before it is too late and we have surrendered control not just of our energy supplies but of our food supplies as well.

subtopic: INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER MET PEQUISTE CANDIDATE
INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER MET PEQUISTE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last November 5 I asked the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) why he had agreed to meet in Montreal Mr. Jacques Desmarais, the PQ candidate in the byelection for the Montreal-Maison-neuve riding. The Prime Minister did not deny that indeed he had met Mr. Desmarais, but he tried to show with his reply that ever since his election to his present position he had tried with his openmindedness and concrete actions to demonstrate to the Quebec population that there is a new administration in Ottawa which is more willing than the former government to meet the legitimate aspirations of the Quebec people.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Prime Minister must be extremely embarrassed to know that the same Mr. Desmarais he met in Montreal lost his election yesterday in a decisive way. There is no doubt that this meeting with the Prime Minister of Canada has not contributed to the good fortune of this PQ candidate; on the contrary, it was probably detrimental to him. On the other hand, the Prime Minister said that he

November 15, 1979
Adjournment Debate
wanted to demonstrate through concrete actions the good faith of his government. Well, the only concrete gestures toward Quebec which the Clark government has made since the election were in areas which only pleased PQ supporters and the Quebec government, and not the federalists and those of them who live in the province of Quebec.
First the Clark government abolished Loto Canada. Second, it got rid of the Tellier working group within the secretariat in charge of federal-provincial relations, the only group which would have been capable of preparing a document seriously and decisively refuting the PQ white paper which advocates Quebec separation. We know now that the Prime Minister does not want to draft a federalist white paper for the Government of Canada which would refute the PQ white paper. Third, the Prime Minister's government has decided not to table the bill providing for a federal referendum, and the Clark government has also instructed federal Crown corporations such as CN and Air Canada not to finance pro-federalist groups in the Quebec referendum campaign.
These are five concrete steps taken by the new Clark government, five concrete steps which in fact have but one aim, namely, to please the Quebec separatists. Mr. Speaker, 1 am asking myself the following question: just what does this Progressive Conservative leader want? When he supposedly takes these concrete steps to please Quebec, he actually does nothing to please the federalists in the province of Quebec, he only pleases the separatists. I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, if this Progressive Conservative leader would not prefer the Parti Quebecois to win the referendum and Quebec to secede from the rest of Canada.
Everything the Prime Minister does and says in the House leads us to that conclusion over any other. Would not this Progressive Conservative leader like to be rid of those 70-odd Liberals from Quebec who sit in the House of Commons, so he could head a majority Progressive Conservative government elected mostly in western Canada, to change the whole political map of Canada? I feel this Progressive Conservative leader is not assuming his responsibilities. He should be looking after the problems of all Canadians, particularly those who live in the province of Quebec, who wish to remain within Canada and who do not approve at all those good will and appeasement gestures the Clark government is making towards the Levesque government in Quebec.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Janelle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER MET PEQUISTE CANDIDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall try to enlighten the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who wanted to change somewhat his question tonight, because he was asking for information about the last August 20 meeting around which there was no mystery and even less secrecy.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) did go to Montreal to meet with businessmen, newspapermen, a well-known Quebec politi-

cian and, finally, a group of workers. More precisely, the Prime Minister met, first, with a group of about ten prominent businessmen of the province of Quebec. The meeting was held in the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, and it is a fact there the economy was discussed.
Secondly, at the same place the Prime Minister met with reporters of the daily newspaper La Presse and if the hon. member wonders about the subjects raised in that interview, all he has to do is read the press reports of the next day. Early in the evening the Prime Minister was the guest of Quebec Premier Levesque for dinner at the Meridien Hotel. The event was in no way secret or mysterious since it had been announced in advance and since it was following the premiers' conference of this summer at La Malbaie. In any case, several reporters interviewed the Prime Minister after his talks with Mr. Levesque.
Finally, before coming back to Ottawa, the Prime Minister met with a group of workers from the port of Montreal who wanted to voice their concerns to him. The meeting took place in a lounge at the Meridien Hotel and Mr. Jacques Desmarais did attend part of that meeting to which he had been invited by the workers. But again, there was nothing secret or mysterious about that meeting since the press was there.
That is what actually happened in Montreal on August 20, 1979, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the hon. member for Papineau will find my answer satisfying.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE-AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-FAIR SHARE FOR CANADA OF CAPITAL INVESTMENT
INTERNATIONAL TRADE-AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-FAIR SHARE FOR CANADA OF CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the preliminary automotive trade figures between Canada and the United States for the first nine months of this year are startling. The over-all Canada-United States trade deficit for this period is $2.2 billion, derived from a favourable balance of $700 million on automotive assembly and a deficit of $2.9 billion on parts. This total deficit exceeds the deficit for the whole of the worst previous year, 1975.
The federal government's sector profile discussion paper of last year indicates that this is part of a developing pattern. 1 quote:
Over the next several years Canadian automotive demand growth will exceed North American demand growth. There will therefore be a trend of long-term deterioration in the automotive trade balance with the United States. A deficit of $2.4 billion (1976 dollars) is projected for 1985 if Canadian production continues to grow at the North American average rate.
Unfortunately, the rate of deterioration in the trade balance has exceeded even this prediction. Already this year it will be beyond the deficit projected for 1985, and the new projection for 1985 by the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association is $5 billion. Without new policies by the federal government, this prediction, too, will be dwarfed by reality.
I congratulate the Progressive Conservative government on continuing and expanding the Liberal policy of duty remissions
November 15, 1979

for foreign companies which will induce additional sourcing of parts in Canada by Volkswagen, Fiat, Nissan, BMW and Mercedes. This will help create more manufacturing jobs in Canada, but it will not help with respect to the parts deficit vis-a-vis the United States, since the companies affected are not American ones. Much more is needed.
The Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association has recently urged the government to encourage investment in the Canadian parts industry, redirect parts sourcing decisions by the automotive companies, stimulate the economy generally, and meet foreign competition. I endorse those proposals.
Investment in the Canadian parts industry could be increased by a repayable loans fund at, say, 1 per cent to 2 per cent over the prime rate-and therefore at a rate competitive with that usually prevailing in the United States-for purposes of investment, tooling, and research in Canada. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. de Cotret) has spoken unfavourably of this proposal by the APMA, but I urge him to reconsider his apparent unwillingness to act on it.
Equally important, in my view, is a policy of inducing the Big Three to source automotive parts in Canada. The fact that the unfavourable exchange rate on Canadian funds is currently causing such a sizeable net loss to the Canadian automotive companies results from undue importation of parts from the United States. Recall if you will, Mr. Speaker, the years 1970, 1971 and 1972, when Canada had a modest over-all automotive trade balance with the United States of $446 million for the three years together. The U.S. government, through then Treasury Secretary Connally, talked tough with the Big Three in the United States-as well as with the Canadian government, incidentally-and succeeded in quickly reversing the incipient trend in our favour.
The United States also introduced the DISC program, a tax incentive plan to promote exports by requiring capital development to be made in the United States to be eligible for the tax advantages.
It is worth noting in passing that the United States government, which has always resisted the Canadian "fair share" interpretation of the auto pact by emphasizing the absolute priority of the free market, hesitated not a moment in interfering with the free market when it appeared that it might advantage Canada rather than themselves.
We need to talk, if not "tough", at least "insistently", with the Big Three with respect to sourcing parts in Canada, and in particular with respect to their own decisions on capital investment for in-house production of parts, as well, of course, as with respect to capital investment for assembly of cars and trucks.
General Motors' new $2 billion investment is most welcome in Canada, particularly in Windsor, but it must not be allowed to represent our total Canadian share of $38 billion of prospective investment.
Adjournment Debate
At the present time in Canada we need an incentive program both for the parts industry and for the economy generally, and in my view and that of my colleagues on this side, no great economic stimulus can be expected while the government keeps interest rates at the highest point in our history and generally follows a tight money policy.
I would also stress the importance of participating more fully in automotive research, development, and engineering. If 1 am right in my guess about Chrysler Canada's proposal to the Canadian government, we are being offered an unequalled opportunity of doing just that, by assisting Chrysler Canada in expanding in that respect. We must take advantage of this opportunity.
I hope these considerations I have advanced on the automotive industry are not taken as partisan ones. These matters are too important, especially in my city of Windsor, where we have at the present time probably the highest rate of unemployment in industrial Canada, to be the prey of mere partisanship.
I genuinely hope the government will solve our problems in the automotive industry. I am prepared to support any reasonable initiatives, whether those I have proposed or others. All I insist is that there should be government initiatives, and soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Huntington (Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE-AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-FAIR SHARE FOR CANADA OF CAPITAL INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be here tonight to hear the representation of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan). 1 realize that this whole subject matter and this industry are very close to him, and he is doing his job here tonight in representing that constituency.
However, may 1 remind the hon. member that many of the problems with which we are faced today are the result of short-term, ad hoc planning, election to election planning in the auto pact and in that industry? I have been told in meetings with the president of the Ford Motor Company, and in meetings with the committee of the Canadian Auto Parts Association that much of our trouble is that we were delivered into the assembly of the high horsepower large automobile, two-thirds of which were shipped to the United States. The energy crunch came in the United States, and that export market dried up on the Canadian assembly plants.
At the same time when the energy crunch hit North America, the United States industry, decisions of which are made in Detroit, had already put in place the energy efficient vehicles for American production so that now two-thirds of the Canadian demand is for American vehicles. That is in large part the problem and the reason for the growth of the deficit in the auto pact that we are dealing with today, and it is a very serious problem for us. We do not take this lightly. I have met with pretty well all sectors of the industry.
I am glad that the phraseology tonight is a little better than the question of the hon. member in the question period as reported in Hansard at page 1082 because I am quite frankly very pleased with the fact that General Motors, without government insistence and without coming to the government

November 15, 1979
Adjournment Debate
for money, was able to deliver $2 billion of capital development in that industry in Canada.
The same thing that I was speaking of in terms of the Auto Pact and the assembly of automobiles in Canada is now going on in the tire industry. We have a tire industry established in Canada exporting tires for the high energy using cars, and yet new technology in tires is now going into the United States, so we are aggravating the problem. We are aware of these problems.
Dealing with the Auto Pact, Mr. Reisman said that the factors which were wrong in the Auto Pact needed renegotiation but the time was not right. I appreciate that. Only last week 1 met with the Auto Parts Association and 1 asked them to come back to me with an agenda of the basic structural flaws that are causing us the problem of the imbalance in the Auto Pact. They have promised to do that.
I do not have to speak on the duty remission program that is in place. It is having an effect and the auto parts industry in Canada is grateful for the benefits that are starting to accrue for them.
One of the problems we have to address and one of the problems we are facing as a nation-again to take the partisanship out of it-is the bidding game that is going on between the United States and Canada for industries, between the states within the United States and the provinces within Canada, as well as between the provinces and the states. This matter will have to be addressed because the bidding game is emptying the public wallet and is interfering with the redistribution and the delivery of resources for the creation of wealth. These are all problems of which we are well aware and I appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Windsor-Walk-erville. We will look for his assistance in resolving some of these problems.
[ Translation]

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEASONAL WORKERS- REQUEST FOR REVISION OF BENEFITS SYSTEM
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEASONAL WORKERS- REQUEST FOR REVISION OF BENEFITS SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the question I put to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Atkey) last October 15 concerning the boundaries of economic zones for unemployment insurance purposes in the Charlevoix area, and following the answer I got then, I thought I would ask the House of Commons for a little more time to listen to the representations I had to make on behalf of the citizens of Charlevoix who are treated unfairly and unduly denied unemployment insurance benefits to which, I think, they are entitled.
Mr. Speaker, last August 24, I sent a letter to the Minister of Employment and Immigration informing him that a group had been established in his department to study the feasibility of changing the boundaries of the Charlevoix economic zone. Right now, Mr. Speaker, to explain the problem more clearly,

the western part of my riding, from Baie Sainte-Catherine to Saint-Fereol-des-Neiges, is included in the metropolitan area of Quebec City which artificially reduces the unemployment rate for that area, while the eastern part of my riding, and 1 am glad of it, Mr. Speaker, and so are the local residents, the eastern part of Tadoussac County up to Hauterive is included in the larger economic area of the north shore where you can get unemployment insurance benefits after ten weeks of work.
Last August 24, as I exchanged correspondence with the Minister of Employment and Immigration, 1 told him that a task force had been established in his department to work on new boundaries for the economic zone to do justice to the residents of Baie Sainte-Catherine, Saint-Simeon, Saint-Fidele, La Malbaie, Pointe-au-Pic, Cap-a-l'Aigle, Clairmont, Notre-Dame-des-Monts and all the other villages in the western part of the constituency, and I wanted to ask him in all sincerity and even urge him to speed up the work of this task force to change the boundaries of economic regions.
Mr. Speaker, my area, Charlevoix West, is essentially dependent on the tourist industry, and as we all know this industry is active only from roughly the second week in June until Labour Day, that is the first week of September, which means that people in the tourist industry work from 11 to 13 weeks a year. Furthermore, in the western part of the Charlevoix constituency, 60 per cent of the labour force is employed in the tourist industry and try as best they can to find a job which will last no more than ten, 11 or 12 weeks. The situation is impossible for these workers who only want a job and not unemployment insurance benefits. Because of the new boundaries of economic regions and since Charlevoix West is included with the Quebec City area, the people who work ten, 11,12 or 13 weeks in the tourist industry, whether for the Manoir Richelieu in Pointe-au-Pic, which employs nearly 300 people, or in the other summer hotels which employ a number of people throughout the constituency, for the first time this year, these people find themselves with no income and must turn to welfare against their own will.
Mr. Speaker, those people are humiliated because they worked during the only period when employment was available to them. Those people have worked and want to work twelve months a year, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately, because of the economic weakness in the area, because of the national economic difficulties, there are no jobs available for 12 months and those people must turn to the tourist industry and work ten, 11 or 12 weeks. So, since this fall, hundreds of people in the riding of Charlevoix have been refused unemployment insurance benefits. I believe that a serious injustice is being caused to people in an underprivileged economic area, and I hope, as the minister already invited me to do in his answer, to suggest to him ways to help those people. He invited me to give my opinion on the situation and also to say what the specific problems in my riding were. I would like tonight on behalf of the people of Charlevoix West to beg him to speed up the work
November 15, 1979

of that study committee within his department that is supposed to change the economic zones in Charlevoix or the economic zone of Charlevoix, and to come up with something in the coming days, Mr. Speaker, because there are people being refused unemployment insurance benefits every day.
I want to beg him to change the economic zone definition which unfairly excludes the people of Charlevoix West because in the months of December, January, February and March, in the riding of Charlevoix, the rate of unemployment easily reaches 35 per cent. Nobody in this House-and 1 am convinced the minister himself is extremely concerned by that situation as I am myself-can be happy with that. I think that notwithstanding Progressive Conservative, Liberal, NDP or Social Credit political considerations, we must try to do justice to those people who only ask to work.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. M. Gurbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SEASONAL WORKERS- REQUEST FOR REVISION OF BENEFITS SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the hon. member for his very sincere representation on behalf of his constituency. The question raised by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Lapointe), which has been raised from time to time by other members, is whether we have the most appropriate and reliable measures for calculating unemployment rates for the unemployment insurance program. This question relates to two issues: first, the drawing of the boundaries of the economic regions for determining initial entitlement for unemployment insurance and for calculating regional extended benefits; second, the method for estimating the unemployment rates.
By way of explanation it should be emphasized that the Unemployment Insurance Act requires that the boundaries of the regions used by Statistics Canada in its labour force survey be followed. The act requires that regional unemployment
Adjournment Debate
rates be those produced by Statistics Canada; Unemployment Insurance Act section 58 (t) and (u). Thus, any change in either respect would require a legislative amendment.
As the minister stated when the matter was raised by the hon. member, a task force representing Statistics Canada and the department has been established to review current arrangements. I confirm that, as soon as the report is received, it will be made available.
Without prejudging the findings of the task force it should be pointed out that there are some obvious difficulties in making changes in the existing arrangements. For example, if boundaries were redrawn to achieve a higher unemployment rate for one region, the adjacent region would experience a corresponding reduction. It may readily be imagined what difficulties this would create.
There are also difficulties in changing the method of calculating unemployment rates, and particularly with the proposal to use unemployment insurance beneficiaries as an indicator of the number of unemployed. Beneficiaries were used in the allocation of Canada Works because labour force survey data are not available on a constituency basis. Moreover, serious questions could be raised about any program which uses its own statistics for the determination of its own entrance requirements and benefit provisions.
An additional consideration is the substantial cost that could be involved in any attempt to enhance the reliability of labour force survey data.
These and other difficulties are being examined by the task force whose report, as indicated, is expected toward the end of November.
